entries.label: Custom Character / Custom Concept
entries.tagline: Type any character, deity, mascot or concept in your own words — the entire production package is built from that text
entries.franchise: the client's own typed description — this entry has NO fixed franchise of its own, and THE DESCRIPTION typed into the Custom Character box is the complete and only identity source. Read it first and decide which of three kinds it is. (a) It NAMES A REAL, WIDELY KNOWN FIGURE — a cartoon character, a deity, a film or mythological role, a sport figure, a known brand mascot: then name that figure and stop. It must be that REAL, ORIGINAL figure exactly as audiences already know it — never a look-alike, never 'inspired by', never a redesign — and add no physical description of your own, because words compete with what the model already knows and produce a generic stand-in instead of the real one. (b) It DESCRIBES AN INVENTED CHARACTER — 'a talking blue auto-rickshaw driver with a handlebar moustache', 'a village grandmother who inspects sarees': then build that character ONCE from the typed nouns and adjectives, honour every concrete detail typed, decide only what the text leaves open, and treat clip 1's build as canon for the rest of the ad. (c) It is A CONCEPT rather than a person — 'the shop's own mascot', 'a mango that talks', 'the spirit of the harvest': then personify it into one consistent character in clip 1 and keep that exact character in every clip after. Whatever is typed is the identity. Never substitute a safer, easier or more familiar character, and never quietly widen a specific description into a generic one.

speakers.name: Custom Character
speakers.voice: characterful in exactly the register THE DESCRIPTION implies — heavy, slow and gravelled for a large, old or powerful figure; bright, quick and high-pitched for a small, young or comic one; calm, resonant and unhurried for a divine or regal one; brisk, warm and street-real for a working-person character — decided at clip 1 and identical in every clip after
speakers.persona: Read entirely out of THE DESCRIPTION. If it names a known figure, use that figure's established, recognisable personality — the traits an audience would list if asked about them — and nothing invented on top. If the character is invented or a concept, derive the personality from the words actually typed: the trade, age, region, size, mood and props each dictate how this character thinks and talks, and anything the text leaves open you settle once, in clip 1, and never revise. Whatever comes out, this character is likeable, energised, and visibly pleased to be showing the viewer this business, and holds that persona in every line. Replace this speaker's display name everywhere with the EXACT name from THE DESCRIPTION, spelled identically in every label, every prompt and every clip.
speakers.scriptRole: Carries the whole ad alone: opens clip 1 with the hook, gives one new and specific real reason to choose the business in each middle clip, and delivers the call to action in the final clip — always in their own register, never as a narrator reading an advertisement. If THE DESCRIPTION names TWO characters, split this role in the order they were typed: the first named opens every clip with the question, reaction or set-up, and the second named answers with the business value and closes the ad. That order is fixed for the entire ad and never reverses.

entries.styleDirective: THE DESCRIPTION decides the render mode, once, and clip 1 locks it for the whole ad. Wording that reads drawn, animated, mascot, toy, puppet or cartoon → a cartoon subject composited into a PHOTOREAL live-action environment: the character stays drawn in every clip, the premises stay photographic and are never restyled around them. Wording that reads human, deity, historical, costumed or celebrity-type → a fully photoreal subject shot on the same lens, grade and colour temperature as the room, with skin, cloth, metal and hair lit by that room's own light. Either way the character stands on the real floor in correct perspective, at a believable size measured against real fixtures — doorway, counter, shelf height — and casts a soft contact shadow matching the direction, hardness and colour of the scene's light. Never switch modes between clips of one ad, and never half-render a subject.
entries.dialogueRhythm: ONE speaker: each clip is a two-part beat inside a single breath — a set-up half that reacts to what is actually on screen, then a pay-off half that lands one business fact. It must sound like a person talking to a friend they dragged along, never a headline read aloud. TWO speakers named in THE DESCRIPTION: the first typed speaks first in every clip and sets up; the second answers with the business value; the order never reverses, both speak in every clip, and the second's line must genuinely ANSWER the first's rather than announce something unrelated. Whichever it is, the last clip is the only one that closes.
entries.voiceDirection: Build one voice from THE DESCRIPTION — its implied age, gender, size, region and mood set the pitch, weight, accent and tempo — and hold that voice unchanged for the entire ad; a voice that shifts between clips reads as a different character. Modulation is scripted, not random: the hook line is the loudest and most surprised, pitched up and slightly rushed; proof lines drop a step, slower and more assured, with the business's real name spoken clearly and never swallowed at the end of a breath; the closing call to action lifts again, warm and direct, spoken as an invitation rather than an instruction. A comic or animated character exaggerates all of this; a divine or elderly character compresses it into calm, weighted delivery with longer pauses. Clean, close, dry studio recording throughout — no reverb, no room tone, no music bed, and no narrator voice appearing at the end to say the tagline.
entries.expressionDirection: Derive the face's resting state from THE DESCRIPTION, then change expression WITH the words, on the exact syllable that carries them — never a single frozen smile held across a clip. Clip 1 opens on genuine surprise: brows up, eyes wide, mouth open on the hook word, settling into delight as the business is named. Middle clips sit in a pleased, convinced half-smile that widens the moment the specific fact lands, with a beat of raised-brow appreciation while looking at the real thing being praised. The final clip is an open, warm, direct-to-viewer smile that reaches the eyes. Scale the range to the character: a comic or mascot figure plays it broad and rubbery; a deity, elder or regal figure compresses it to benevolent calm at rest with a slight knowing smile on the pay-off and no comedy at all; a working-person character plays it straight and real. The underlying face — its structure, age, markings and proportions — never changes between clips; only the expression on it does.
entries.eyeDirection: The eyes go where the words go. While the line praises a real thing in the room, the gaze is ON that thing — the shelf, the machine, the stock, the counter — and the head follows a beat behind the eyes, never together. On the reaction and on the reason-to-buy, the gaze comes back to the lens (or to the second character, if THE DESCRIPTION named one). The closing call to action is delivered looking straight down the lens, holding it unblinking for the final beat. Blinks fall naturally between phrases, never on an emphasis word. Pupils sized to the room's actual light, catchlights matching the practical lights visible in frame. No dead or glassy stare, no wandering or crossed eyes, no eyes drifting off-frame mid-sentence. With two characters, each looks at whoever is speaking and the listener's eyes stay live and reacting rather than idling.
entries.gestureDirection: One clear gesture per line, begun and completed inside the clip — never a hand frozen mid-air at the cut. Take the gesture vocabulary from THE DESCRIPTION itself: open palm-up presenting hands for a warm host character; a raised index finger for a know-it-all; a blessing or open-palm abhaya hand for a divine figure; the actual tools, cloth, produce or instrument a working character would be holding; and whatever non-human parts the text specifies — trunk, tail, wings, extra arms — used naturally and counted identically in every clip. On proof lines the hand indicates the REAL object in frame with an open palm turned towards it, never a stiff finger poked at empty space. On the closing line both hands open outward to the viewer in an invitation. No fidgeting, no repeating the same gesture twice in a row, no hand crossing or covering the face, and no gesture that a character with these hands could not physically make.
entries.bodyLanguage: Weight always grounded and readable. Clip 1, arrival: turned a quarter into the room, chest open, weight on the front foot as if they have just walked in and are taking the place in. Middle clips: relaxed and angled towards the thing being talked about, a small natural weight shift on each new fact, leaning in slightly on the strongest claim. Final clip: squared to the viewer, shoulders open, both feet planted. Scale stays honest across the whole ad — the same height relative to the doorway, counter and shelves in every clip. Posture follows THE DESCRIPTION: a heavy or elderly character moves slowly with settled weight; a small or comic one is springy and quick; a divine or regal one is upright, still and unhurried. All movement is small and human-real — no bouncing, dancing, swaying, hovering, and no full walk across the frame inside an eight-second clip.
entries.cameraDirection: Clip 1: a wide establishing shot at the entrance or shopfront, the character full-figure with the business clearly readable behind, camera at that character's own eye level — or slightly low if THE DESCRIPTION implies a tall, heroic or divine figure, which is never shot down on. Middle clips: medium and medium-close shots, one fresh angle and one fresh zone each time, using the room's real lines — counters, aisles, door frames — to build depth, with the equipment or stock the line is about clearly beside or behind the subject. Final clip: a clean, slightly wider, warm frame back at the entrance or main counter with the business unmistakable around them. Inside a clip the camera holds steady as one continuous shot — at most a slow push-in or a gentle handheld float; no whip pans, no orbits, no cuts, no crash zooms. Compose for the ordered aspect ratio only: eyes on the upper third, headroom tight, the subject filling roughly sixty to seventy percent of the frame, and never a composition borrowed from a different ratio.
entries.backgroundDirection: When no client photographs are attached, build a photoreal, currently-operating Indian business of exactly this trade from the business profile — real stock on real shelving, real fixtures, working practical lights, honest wear on the floor and counters. Never a showroom render, never an empty studio set, never a foreign-looking interior, and never blank walls, empty frames or placeholder boards. Every clip is set in a DIFFERENT zone, and the zone is chosen so the background PROVES that clip's line: product range → the shelves; service or price → the billing counter; expertise → the work area or workshop; welcome and call to action → the entrance. Light each zone plausibly for where it sits in the building — daylight spilling from the shopfront at the entrance, warmer artificial light deeper inside — and keep one consistent grade across all clips so they read as one visit. The environment is never restyled to suit the character: a cartoon subject does not turn the shop into a cartoon, and a deity does not turn it into a temple. When the client's photographs ARE attached, they are the ground truth — reproduce the real architecture, stock, signage and light, match the photo's camera level, and stage the character into it rather than redesigning it.
entries.scriptStyle: Written in the character's own register but ABOUT the business, always. The first line is a hook that stops a scroll — surprise at something in front of them, an unanswered question, the customer's own problem, or open disbelief at a claim — never a greeting, never 'today I will tell you about', never anything a narrator would say. The business's real name is spoken early and repeated; the character's own name is spoken at most ONCE in the entire ad, in clip 1, and never again, because every word spent on the character is a word the client did not get. Each middle clip carries exactly ONE new, specific, real thing this business offers, taken only from the business information — never a benefit already used, never a claim that would fit any other shop. Apply the generic test to every line and rewrite any line that could belong to another business. Never invent a price, offer, year, address or service; never speak digits; never speak a phone number. Only the final clip carries the call to action, and it must feel finished rather than interrupted. Every line is one complete sentence inside the clip's word budget — shorten the thought, never cut a sentence in half. Write in the ad's chosen language as it is really spoken, not as it is written in books; if the character's name is spoken at all, lock one spelling in clip 1 and reuse those exact characters everywhere.
negatives: Do NOT substitute a different, safer or more familiar character — THE DESCRIPTION is the only identity, and a named existing figure must be that REAL figure, never a look-alike, an 'inspired by' redesign, or a generic Indian cartoon man or woman

Do NOT drift the design between clips — clip 1's build, face, costume, colours, markings and proportions are canon; re-describing the character in later prompts is exactly what makes it change, so refer back to the locked reference frame instead
Do NOT mix render modes — a cartoon subject stays fully drawn in every clip and a photoreal subject stays fully photographic; never a drawn face on a photographed body or the reverse
Do NOT restyle, cartoonify, tidy, modernise or upgrade the premises to suit the character — the location stays photoreal exactly as it is
No additional characters of any kind — no sidekick, mascot, crowd, passer-by or staff member that THE DESCRIPTION did not name
No prop, costume, vehicle, weapon, jewellery or accessory that the description did not specify, and nothing specified may change, appear or disappear between clips
Keep non-human anatomy exactly as described and identical in every clip — the same count of arms, hands, tails, trunks, wings, horns or eyes, never gained or lost
If THE DESCRIPTION names a living real person, do not attempt their photographic likeness — build the character the description implies instead
No narrator, no second voice, no dubbing accent, and no voice change partway through — one fixed voice for the whole ad

Do NOT make the character the subject of the ad — the business is what is being sold; no meta-talk about characters, videos, advertising, marketing or promotion unless that is literally this client's trade
No on-screen text, captions, subtitles, logos-as-text, or watermarks — and never render the typed description, the character's name, or any label into the frame
No floating subject — the character must contact the ground with matching shadows
No morphing, no extra or missing limbs, no distorted faces
No background music — clean studio voice only

entries.label: Normal Ad (Female)
entries.tagline: The default polished female presenter, filmed inside the client's real premises
entries.franchise: No franchise and no borrowed character. A newly cast Indian female brand ambassador, strictly 20-25, of the tier you would see fronting a Lakme / Tanishq / Malabar Gold national television commercial - one unique face invented for THIS client, locked from clip 1 and reused unchanged for the whole campaign. Never a look-alike of a named actress, never the same recurring ad face two clients in a row, never an ethnically ambiguous global stock model.

speakers.name: Presenter
speakers.voice: warm, bright and precisely articulated, mid-to-high register with unhurried premium-television polish
speakers.persona: A poised young Indian brand ambassador who speaks for the business as if she has actually used it - confident without hard-selling, warm without being girlish, articulate, and completely at ease on camera.
speakers.scriptRole: She carries the entire ad alone. Clip 1 she hooks the viewer and names the business and its town; each middle clip she delivers exactly one concrete proof point; the final clip she gives the reason to act now and the call to action. There is no second voice at any point.

entries.styleDirective: One photoreal Indian woman, 20-25, alone in frame, standing inside the client's REAL business premises and shot like a national television commercial. She wears either a premium tailored formal suit (structured blazer, crisp white inner shirt, slim formal trousers) or a designer silk saree with a modest elbow-length blouse, in a colour pulled from the client's logo palette. Hair is rich natural black with a professional blowout finish. She occupies roughly 70% of the frame height and stands one and a half to two metres clear of the fixtures so both she and the premises read cleanly. Skin keeps visible pores, micro-texture and truthful Indian complexion under camera-ready makeup. Same woman, same face, same wardrobe, same hair in every clip - only the zone of the premises changes.
entries.dialogueRhythm: Single speaker, no second voice, no cutaway. Each 8-second clip is ONE complete spoken thought delivered straight to the lens: a two-second lead-in, the substance across the middle four, and a settled final beat where she stops speaking and holds the smile for roughly half a second before the cut. A sentence never trails across a clip boundary, and she never begins a gesture she cannot finish inside the clip.
entries.voiceDirection: Warm, bright and cleanly articulated at a steady presenter pace of about 2.2 words per second - never rushed, never breathless. Pitch lifts slightly on the business name and on any offer figure, then drops into a lower, softer, more confident register for the closing call to action. Clean studio voice with no reverb tail, no whisper-breathiness, no sing-song advertising lilt, and no dropping away at the end of sentences.
entries.expressionDirection: She enters every clip already smiling - a genuine warm smile that reaches the eyes and creates faint natural laugh lines, never a held corporate rictus. The smile softens into sincere, attentive near-neutral while she states a factual proof (price, timing, guarantee), then reopens fully across the last three words of the clip. Brows lift a few millimetres on the surprise or offer beat and settle immediately after. In the closing clip the smile is the widest of the whole ad and holds through the final beat.
entries.eyeDirection: Direct, unbroken eye contact into the lens in every clip - never into the distance, never at the products, never at an off-camera reader. Blinks are single and soft, roughly one every 3-4 seconds, never a rapid flutter and never a locked unblinking stare. Where she gestures toward something in the premises, the eyes may flick to it for under half a second and must be back on the lens before the next word. Iris stays deep dark brown with a natural limbal ring and a single clean catchlight; no glassy, dead or drifting gaze.
entries.gestureDirection: Clip 1 is the formal front-clasp: both hands at the lower waist, right hand resting lightly over the left, fingers relaxed and partly overlapping, no gesture at all. From clip 2 the hands unlock and each clip earns exactly ONE clear, unhurried movement matched to that line - an open palm presenting the counter or equipment beside her, a soft downward accent on a number, a light touch on a real surface, and in the closing clip both palms opening outward in an inviting 'come to us'. Gestures live between the waist and the sternum, fingers together and anatomically correct, never above the shoulders, never crossing the face, never pointing at the viewer, and each returns to rest before the clip ends.
entries.bodyLanguage: Standing tall, shoulders square to camera in clip 1, chin level, weight settled through both feet with the relaxed ease of someone who has done a hundred photoshoots - never at attention, never mannequin-stiff. From clip 2 the torso takes a gentle 10-15 degree angle into the room while the face stays square to the lens, one shoulder slightly forward and weight shifted onto the back foot. Between phrases only small believable settling: no swaying, no rocking, no repositioning the feet mid-line, no hip-out fashion posing.
entries.cameraDirection: 9:16 vertical throughout. Clip 1: locked-off medium-full / three-quarter standing shot, lens at her chest level, dead-centre framing with balanced left-right space and the reception clearly readable behind her. From clip 2, one close mid-shot per clip (head to upper waist) with a deliberate and different treatment each time - a slow 3-5% push-in across the 8 seconds, a slight low angle from just below chest for the showcase beat, a gentle 10-15 degree three-quarter with the logo wall in soft depth for the trust beat. All motion is slow and motivated: no handheld shake, no whip pans, no orbiting, no snap zooms, and no cut inside a clip. Soft key from camera-left with clean fill, matched to the premises' own colour temperature.
entries.backgroundDirection: When the client sends no photographs, build the real, operational premises of that exact sector - a working showroom floor, clinic reception, workshop, service counter or office a customer would actually walk into - and reuse the SAME establishment in every clip, changing only which functional zone she stands in: reception first, then the real work or stock area, then the branded logo wall for the trust beat, then a further distinct zone, and back near the entrance to close. The chosen zone must visually prove the exact line she is speaking. Never a home interior, living room, bedroom, hotel lobby, empty coworking corner or anonymous studio backdrop; never wood-panelled or plank walls; never invented certificate, award, achievement or photo walls. The client's logo appears once, installed flat on a wall sign or reception panel facing camera.
entries.scriptStyle: Straight, respectful spokesperson copy - she is the business talking to a customer, not a comedian and not a hype reel. Clip 1 hooks on the customer's own problem and names the business and its town in the same breath; each middle clip carries exactly one real, specific benefit drawn from the business information and never repeats an earlier one; the final clip gives the reason to act now plus the call to action. Everyday spoken sentences, six to fourteen words, short enough to breathe inside 8 seconds - no rhymes, no slogans, no English marketing jargon dropped into the regional language, no superlatives the business cannot back up.
negatives: No on-screen text, captions, subtitles, logos-as-text, or watermarks
No floating subject - she must contact the floor with a shadow that matches the scene's light
No morphing, no extra or missing limbs, no distorted faces
No background music - clean studio voice only
No second person anywhere in frame - no staff, no customers, no reflected or background humans; she is alone
Do NOT change her face, hair, wardrobe colour or jewellery between clips - one identity for the whole campaign
No hair colour other than natural rich black - no brown, auburn, burgundy, copper, highlights or lighting-induced colour shift
No sleeveless, spaghetti-strap or deep-cut blouse, no casual wear, no spectacles, no bridal or festival costume in a commercial ad
No beauty-filter skin, plastic smoothing, waxy highlights or over-symmetrical AI face - keep visible pores and micro-texture
No looking away from the lens, no gaze drifting to products or off-camera
No non-Indian, ethnically ambiguous, westernised or generic global stock-model casting
No home interiors, hotel lobbies, wood-panelled walls, or invented certificate, award or photo walls behind her

entries.label: Normal Ad (Male)
entries.tagline: The default polished male presenter, filmed inside the client's real premises
entries.franchise: No franchise and no borrowed character. A newly cast Indian male brand ambassador, strictly 30-35, of the tier you would see in a premium menswear or grooming national television commercial - one unique face created for THIS client and held identical across every clip. Never an imitation of a named actor, never the recurring stock ad face, never ethnically ambiguous or westernised casting.

speakers.name: Presenter
speakers.voice: deep, calm and resonant, a clean baritone with unhurried diction and quiet authority
speakers.persona: A composed Indian businessman-presenter in his early thirties who speaks like the person actually accountable for the service - assured, straightforward, quietly proud of the business, reassuring rather than excitable.
speakers.scriptRole: He is the only voice in the ad. Clip 1 he hooks the viewer and names the business and its town; each middle clip states one factual proof; the final clip carries the reason to come now and the call to action. No second speaker exists in this format.

entries.styleDirective: One photoreal Indian man, 30-35, alone in frame inside the client's REAL business premises, lit and framed like a premium menswear commercial. Wardrobe is a well-tailored formal suit or a sharp shirt-and-trouser combination in a tone drawn from the client's logo palette, with a classic wristwatch, polished formal shoes, and at most one slim formal ring - no necklace, no earrings, no other jewellery. Hair is natural black, neatly cut and groomed; either clean-shaven or a tightly trimmed even beard, held identical in every clip. Skin stays matte with real pores and texture - no makeup look, no lip sheen, no smoothing. He fills roughly 70% of frame height and stands clear of the fixtures so both he and the premises read.
entries.dialogueRhythm: Single speaker, no second voice. Each 8-second clip is one complete statement to camera, delivered slower than the female presenter - about 2 words per second - with a deliberate half-beat pause placed just before the most important noun in the line. He finishes with roughly a second of clip left, holds the look, and the cut lands on that hold. No sentence carries over into the next clip.
entries.voiceDirection: Baritone, calm, level and chest-resonant with clean consonants and no vocal fry. Volume stays even throughout; emphasis comes from slowing down and pausing rather than getting louder. Warm on the opening greeting, flat-and-factual through the proof points, firm with a slight downward inflection on the call to action. Clean studio voice - no reverb, no smiling sing-song, no radio-jockey energy, and no rising question intonation on statements.
entries.expressionDirection: He opens on a controlled closed-lip confident smile - friendly, never toothy - and holds a steady assured face through the factual lines. The smile becomes a genuine open smile exactly twice in the ad: on the business name in clip 1, and across the whole closing call to action. One small confirming nod lands on the key benefit word in each middle clip. Brows stay level and relaxed throughout; no eyebrow theatrics, no smirk, no salesman grin, no blank stone face.
entries.eyeDirection: Level, locked eye contact into the lens for the whole of every clip - never up, never down, never toward an unseen reader. Blinks are slow and single, roughly one every 4 seconds, and never during the last two words of a line. When a hand presents something in the premises the eyes may travel to it for at most half a second and must return to the lens before he speaks again. The gaze reads steady and trustworthy, never staring, never aggressive, never vacant.
entries.gestureDirection: Clip 1: hands still - relaxed at his sides or lightly clasped in front at waist level, no gesture, the stance carries the shot. From clip 2 each clip earns exactly one restrained business gesture between waist and chest: an open upward palm presenting the work area, a single downward beat of the hand on a figure or promise, a light hand resting on a real counter, and two palms opening in invitation on the closing clip. Fingers stay together and anatomically correct, elbows stay close to the body, nothing rises above the shoulders or crosses the face, and each gesture returns to rest before the line ends. Never point at the camera, never a thumbs-up, never hands in pockets.
entries.bodyLanguage: Upright and grounded, feet a shoulder's width apart, weight even, shoulders relaxed and squared to camera in clip 1 with the chin level - authoritative, never a soldier's brace. From clip 2 the torso takes a shallow 10-15 degree turn into the room while the face stays to the lens, one foot slightly forward. Movement between phrases is minimal: a small settle of the shoulders, and a slight lean in on the single most important sentence of the ad. No pacing, no rocking, no repeated weight shifts, no crossed arms at any point.
entries.cameraDirection: 9:16 vertical throughout. Clip 1: locked-off medium-full standing shot, lens at chest level and fractionally below his eye line so he reads with stature, centred with balanced spacing and the reception legible behind him. From clip 2, one close mid-shot per clip with a distinct treatment - a slow 4% push-in on the strongest proof line, a slight low angle for the work-area beat, a gentle three-quarter with the logo wall in soft depth for the trust beat. Depth of field separates him from the room without making the business unreadable. All camera movement slow and motivated: no handheld shake, no snap zooms, no orbiting, no cut within a clip. Key light slightly harder than the female treatment, from camera-right, with a controlled fill that keeps the jaw defined.
entries.backgroundDirection: With no client photographs, construct the honest working premises of that trade at the scale such a business really has, and hold the SAME establishment across all clips while moving him through it: the entrance or front counter to open, then the service desk, then the live work or stock floor, then the branded name-board wall, and back to the entrance to close. Each zone must be the visual proof of that clip's spoken line, and each clip must use a zone not yet seen. Never a home interior, apartment, bedroom, hotel lobby or anonymous coworking corner; never timber-panelled, plank or log-cabin walls; never invented certificate, accreditation, award or photo walls. The logo or name board appears once only, physically mounted on a flat wall facing the camera with believable material depth.
entries.scriptStyle: Plain, confident, third-person spokesperson copy - he speaks about the business as its representative, in the language a customer hears across the counter. Clip 1 opens on the problem the customer already has and names the business and its town in one breath; each middle clip carries exactly one factual, checkable benefit and never repeats one already used; the last clip gives a reason to come now plus the call to action. Short declarative sentences of six to fourteen words - no rhymes, no slogans, no stacked adjectives, no English marketing jargon inside the regional language, and no claim the business information does not support.
negatives: No on-screen text, captions, subtitles, logos-as-text, or watermarks
No floating subject - he must contact the floor with a shadow that matches the scene's light
No morphing, no extra or missing limbs, no distorted faces
No background music - clean studio voice only
Do NOT feminise the styling - no makeup look, no lipstick, no kajal, no necklace, no earrings, no bangles, no bindi
No second person in frame - no staff, no customers, no background or reflected humans
No change of face, hairstyle, beard shape or wardrobe between clips - one identity for the whole campaign
No hands in pockets, no crossed arms, no pointing at the camera, no thumbs-up
No casual wear, t-shirts, kurta-pyjama, sunglasses or spectacles
No over-smoothed plastic skin and no de-aged boyish face - he must read as a man of 30 to 35 with real skin texture and a defined jaw
No non-Indian, ethnically ambiguous, westernised or generic global stock-model casting

entries.label: Real Owner Face (Male)
entries.tagline: The client's own face from his photograph, held 100% identical in every clip
entries.franchise: There is no character here and nothing to cast: the identity is the REAL business owner in the photograph the client supplied, and that single photograph is the only source of truth for his face. Treat the reference the way a portrait photographer treats the person sitting in front of the lens - the job is to photograph THIS man inside his own business, never to cast someone who resembles him. If a customer who knows him would hesitate for even a moment about whether that is him, the frame has failed.

speakers.name: Business Owner
speakers.voice: his own natural adult male register - grounded, sincere and conversational, the voice of a proprietor talking across his counter rather than an announcer
speakers.persona: The real owner speaking for himself. Proud of what he has built, direct, plainspoken, a little warm, and credible precisely because he is the person the customer will actually meet when they walk in.
speakers.scriptRole: He is the only person on screen and speaks in the FIRST PERSON throughout. Clip 1 he introduces himself and names his business; each middle clip he gives one concrete thing he does for the customer; the final clip is his personal invitation to come and meet him.

entries.styleDirective: One photoreal human being - the exact man in the client's reference photograph - standing inside his own business premises. His face is carried from the reference at 100% fidelity: the SAME facial structure, SAME eye shape and eye spacing, SAME nose, SAME mouth and lip shape, SAME jaw and cheekbones, SAME apparent age with every existing line and fold intact, SAME skin tone and skin texture including marks, moles and scars, SAME hairline, hair density and hair colour including any grey, and the SAME moustache or beard shape, in every single frame of every single clip. Where the reference is only head-and-shoulders, complete the body plausibly for his visible build and dress him in ONE clean formal shirt or business outfit chosen once and never changed - but nothing above the collar may be reinterpreted, softened or improved. Identity must never drift between clip 1 and the final frame.
entries.dialogueRhythm: Single speaker in first person, one clip one thought. He speaks at a natural, unhurried conversational pace with a real breath before the first word and small honest pauses where a person would actually pause - this is a business owner talking, not a script being read. Every line must be LIP-SYNC FRIENDLY: short sentences, open vowels, clear consonants, no tongue-twisters, no long compound words, no strings of digits, and nothing that cannot be finished comfortably inside 8 seconds at a relaxed pace. He finishes with about a second of clip left and holds a calm closed-mouth expression through the cut.

entries.label: Lord Ganesha
entries.tagline: Vighna-harta blesses the business — warm, auspicious, obstacles cleared before the work begins
entries.franchise: Lord Ganesha (Ganapati / Vinayaka) of Hindu tradition — the elephant-headed remover of obstacles, son of Shiva and Parvati, as worshipped in South Indian temples and painted in Indian devotional calendar art. His fixed emblems and no others: four arms carrying pasha (noose) and ankusha (goad) in the upper hands, abhaya mudra in the lower right and a bowl of modakas in the lower left; the broken right tusk; the curled trunk turning to his left; red-and-gold silks, a heavy gold crown and rudraksha-and-gold ornaments; the small mouse Mushika at his feet. Reach for the real, first-worshipped Ganesha of the sanctum, never a decorative idol or an artist's reinvention.

speakers.name: Ganesha
speakers.voice: deep, warm and unhurried, with a gentle smile inside it
speakers.persona: The beloved god who is asked first and clears the road before any work begins — affectionate, approachable, endlessly patient, quietly amused by how much people worry. He reassures rather than commands. Warmth is his power: nothing he says is anxious, sharp or hurried, and nothing he says is a joke.
speakers.scriptRole: Speaks the entire ad alone, to the viewer. Clip 1 he names the obstacle standing in the customer's way — the worry, the delay, the thing that keeps going wrong. Each middle clip takes ONE real thing this business actually does and gives it as that obstacle removed. The final clip is a blessing on the business and its family that carries the invitation to come — the blessing IS the call to action. He never states a price, never speaks digits or a phone number, and never says 'buy'.

entries.styleDirective: A hyper-realistic, fully three-dimensional living murti — temple stone and gold made flesh, with real skin texture on the trunk and ears, real weight in the gold ornaments, real silk that hangs. Never a flat calendar print, never a plastic 3D render, never a game cinematic, never a cartoon. He is composited at larger-than-human scale into a PHOTOREAL Indian business interior, which is never restyled or beautified around him: he sits on a low ornate seat that rests on the actual floor, in correct perspective, casting a soft warm contact shadow that matches the room's own light. A warm amber divine glow radiates from him and spills believably onto the real fixtures nearest him — the counter edge, the shelf lip, the floor — so he is lighting the room rather than pasted onto it. A low, thin drift of sandal smoke at floor level; fresh marigold and a banana leaf of modakas placed where a shopkeeper would really place them.
entries.dialogueRhythm: One thought per clip, delivered in two unhurried movements: first the human difficulty named plainly, then the relief. He lands the last word and then rests — the silence at the end of every clip is part of the blessing and must not be trimmed. No rhetorical questions, no rising urgency, no line that runs into the next clip. Every clip ends more settled than it began.
entries.voiceDirection: Deep, rounded, paternal bass-baritone at a slow, generous pace — roughly two-thirds the speed of a normal ad read. The smile is audible in the vowels; the consonants are soft, never percussive. Volume stays even from the first word to the last: no build, no emphasis spikes, no dramatic drop before the blessing. A small natural room tail as if recorded inside a stone sanctum, and nothing more — no processed reverb, no pitch-shifting, no elephant sounds of any kind. Never booming, never theatrical, never the voice of a narrator selling something.
entries.expressionDirection: A settled, benevolent half-smile held from first frame to last, with the eyes softly creased at the corners. The face changes exactly twice in the whole ad: on the obstacle line the brow lowers a fraction into shared concern — the look of someone who already knows your trouble — and it releases back into the smile on the word that resolves it; then at the final blessing the smile widens by a few millimetres and no more. The change must be small enough that a viewer feels it rather than sees it. The trunk stays relaxed in its curve and never animates for expression; the ears never flap; the mouth never opens wide.
entries.eyeDirection: A warm, direct gaze into the lens on every reassurance and every blessing line — he is looking at the devotee, not past them. Blinks are slow, deliberate and rare, no more than two in a clip. Exactly once per ad, on the line that names the business, he lets his eyes travel unhurriedly across the real premises around him and come back to the lens, as an elder taking in a house he approves of. The eyes never dart, never flick to the side, never look down and never break contact mid-sentence.
entries.gestureDirection: One completed gesture per clip, made slowly and then HELD — never a hand moving to punctuate words. The lower right hand rises into abhaya mudra (palm forward, fingers up, at chest level) on the reassurance line and stays there for the rest of the clip. The lower left holds the modaka bowl absolutely still. The upper hands hold pasha and ankusha upright and steady and never gesture with them at all. The trunk curls slightly to his left and stays. He never points at, touches, holds or presents the client's products, never handles money, a phone or a card machine, and never mimes a shopkeeper's actions.
entries.bodyLanguage: Seated in relaxed lalitasana on a low ornate seat — one leg folded, the other foot resting flat on the actual floor, weight fully settled, spine easy rather than rigid. Shoulders broad and low. The body barely moves through the whole clip: a single slight settling of the shoulders on the blessing line is the entire performance. He never leans towards the camera, never rocks, never shifts weight, never rises, never dances. Mushika stays at his foot on the ground, still and alert, and is never posed for cuteness.
entries.cameraDirection: Camera at chest level, a hair below his eye line, so the viewer looks slightly up at him the way a devotee does. 50mm-equivalent, shallow but not creamy. Each clip opens with one gentle vertical tilt-up from the modaka bowl to his face, then a slow 6–8 second push-in that finishes on a chest-up frame exactly as the blessing lands, and locks there. Locked-off on sticks between moves. No handheld, no whip pan, no orbit, no crash zoom, no drone move, and never a shot looking down at him from above.
entries.backgroundDirection: The client's own photographs always win — these settings are only for frames that must be generated. With no photos, build a warm, real, working Indian premises of the client's own trade and dress it with an auspicious threshold: deep vermilion and gold, a fresh mango-leaf and marigold torana over the doorway, a row of lit brass diyas at floor level, kumkum and turmeric on a brass plate, a haze of sandal smoke. Amber-warm key light coming from lamp level and rising, so the glow sits low in the frame. The place must look operating and lived-in — real stock, real wear, real counters — never an empty studio set, never a temple that replaces the business.
entries.scriptStyle: Written as a blessing, not a pitch. First person, spoken directly to the viewer and to the owner of the business. Short declarative sentences of eight to twelve spoken words, each one complete on its own. The vocabulary is the vocabulary of obstacles removed, of beginnings made auspicious, of work that prospers and a house that stays full — but the sentences stay SPOKEN, everyday and clear, never scriptural, never chanted, never a stotram. The business's real name is said once, with respect, the way an elder names a family. Each middle clip carries one true, specific thing the business actually offers, stated plainly; the deity never guarantees or personally endorses a product — he blesses the effort and the people, and the ad states the facts. The close is a benediction that doubles as the invitation to come. No slang, no superlatives, no jokes, no exclamation.

Never a realistic zoo elephant head and never a human head — the canonical murti head, with the broken right tusk always present
The four arms of his canonical form are correct and required — never three, never six, never a pair of arms dropped or added between clips
Never mix iconography — no trident, no damaru, no snake, no third eye, no crescent moon, no peacock feather, no flute anywhere near him; only his own emblems
No other deity, no priest, no worshipper, no crowd and no human figure anywhere in frame
He never holds, touches, points at or presents the client's products, and never handles cash, a card machine or a phone
Never eating, chewing or reaching for the modakas — the bowl is held, not used

No morphing, no extra or missing limbs, no distorted faces

entries.label: Goddess Lakshmi
entries.tagline: Sri Lakshmi blesses the business — serene, golden, prosperity that stays
entries.franchise: Goddess Lakshmi (Sri Mahalakshmi) of Hindu tradition — consort of Vishnu, giver of wealth, fortune and abundance, as worshipped in South Indian temples and painted in Indian devotional calendar art. Her fixed emblems and no others: four arms, the upper two holding open red lotuses, the lower right in varada mudra with a slow steady fall of gold coins from the open palm, the lower left in abhaya mudra; standing or seated on a full-blown pink lotus; deep red or golden-yellow Kanchipuram silk with heavy zari; full temple gold — vaddanam, haaram, kasula peru, nose ring and a tall gold crown; a pair of white elephants only if the frame calls for the Gaja-Lakshmi form. Reach for the real Mahalakshmi of the sanctum, never a model in costume.

speakers.name: Lakshmi
speakers.voice: serene, clear and softly resonant, like a boon being given
speakers.persona: The goddess who enters a house that is kept well and stays where there is honesty — composed, maternal, unhurried, entirely without urgency because nothing she promises is in doubt. She gives rather than persuades. Her warmth is steady and even, never effusive, never sweet, never coaxing.
speakers.scriptRole: Speaks the entire ad alone, to the viewer. Clip 1 she recognises the shop and the family who keep it — she has come because the work here is honest. Each middle clip takes ONE real thing this business offers and gives it as abundance the customer takes home and keeps, never as a bargain. The final clip is a boon on the household and the shop together, ending in the invitation to come. She never states a price, never speaks digits or a phone number, and never says 'offer', 'discount' or 'cheap'.

entries.styleDirective: A hyper-realistic, fully three-dimensional living murti — real skin with true subsurface warmth, real gold with real weight and real reflections, silk that falls and folds under gravity. Never a flat calendar print, never a plastic 3D render, never a cartoon. She is composited at slightly larger-than-human scale into a PHOTOREAL Indian business interior that is never restyled around her: the lotus she stands on rests on the actual floor in correct perspective, casting a soft, warm contact shadow that matches the room's own light. A soft golden radiance comes off her and lands believably on the real surfaces closest to her — the counter top, the glass of a display case, the floor tiles — with a fine drift of gold-lit dust in the air. The falling coins land and rest near the lotus; they never pile up over the client's goods and never turn the premises into a treasure room.
entries.dialogueRhythm: One flowing thought per clip, even from the first word to the last, like a stream that does not change pace. Every clip ends on a gently rising, giving note — the sound of something being granted, not something being concluded. No pauses inside a line; one short, calm rest at the end of each clip. She never asks a question, never repeats a word for emphasis, and never quickens.
entries.voiceDirection: A clear, serene female mezzo, softly resonant and even in volume throughout. Long, smooth vowels; consonants placed gently. Each sentence closes on a small upward inflection so it reads as a boon being given rather than a statement being made. The pace is unhurried and identical in every clip — no build, no emphasis spikes. A light natural room tail as if recorded in a stone hall. Never breathy, never seductive, never girlish, never bright and chirpy, never a friendly retail voice-over.
entries.expressionDirection: Serene, unwavering compassion held throughout — lips closed in a faint smile, brow completely smooth, no tension anywhere in the face. The expression changes exactly twice: it softens further, with a barely visible lowering of the eyelids, on the line about the family who run the business; and it brightens minutely on the final boon, the smile reaching the eyes without the lips parting. Her mouth never opens wide, she never laughs, never raises an eyebrow, never registers surprise or concern. Whatever the line, the face stays composed — that composure is the character.
entries.eyeDirection: The classic murti gaze: eyes half-lowered, looking gently down and then forward so she meets the devotee slightly from above. She rests her eyes on the lens for the whole of every giving line and does not break away. The lids lower slowly at the end of each sentence and lift again as the next begins — that slow lid movement is her only eye motion. Blinks are few, slow and complete. Never a sideways glance, never a darting look, never a wide stare, never eyes following the coins.
entries.gestureDirection: Her hands do not punctuate her speech at all — the stillness of the upper body is the whole point. The upper right and upper left hands hold their red lotuses upright and motionless. The lower left holds abhaya mudra (palm forward, fingers up) from the first frame to the last without moving. The lower right stays open in varada mudra, angled down, and gold coins fall from it in a slow, continuous, gentle stream — a steady fall, never a burst, never a shower, never speeding up on a strong line. She never points at, holds or presents the client's products, never touches money other than the coins that fall from her own palm, and never handles a phone, card machine or cash box.
entries.bodyLanguage: Standing (or seated in padmasana) on a full-blown lotus, weight perfectly balanced on both feet, spine straight, shoulders open and level, chin neither raised nor dropped. The silk hangs still; the gold does not swing. The entire body is at rest for the whole clip — no sway, no weight shift, no step, no turn towards camera, no lean. Nothing moves in frame except her mouth, her eyelids and the falling coins. If the Gaja-Lakshmi form is used, the two white elephants stand still and symmetrical behind her and never move.
entries.cameraDirection: A slow rise: begin at floor level on the lotus and its shadow, and crane or tilt up over about ten seconds to a chest-up frame, then hold absolutely still for the rest of the clip. 85mm-equivalent for clean separation, with the falling coins kept in focus. A very slight lateral drift is permitted during the hold and nothing more. Frame her centred and symmetrical, camera just below her eye line. No handheld, no orbit, no push-in, no rack focus, no crash zoom, and never a shot looking down at her from above.
entries.backgroundDirection: The client's own photographs always win — these settings are only for frames that must be generated. With no photos, build the real premises of the client's own trade at first light and give it an abundance dressing: gold-lit pillared depth behind her, brass kalashams overflowing with unhusked rice and mango leaves, a low heap of rice and a scatter of gold ornaments on red silk, fresh lotuses, a lit ghee lamp. Warm golden backlight from behind her with a soft fill from the front, so the air itself glows and the shadows stay open. speakers.name: Durga
speakers.voice: commanding, chest-strong and absolutely steady
speakers.persona: The mother who stands between her people and whatever threatens them — decisive, immovable, without a trace of doubt. Her power is expressed as certainty, never as anger. speakers.scriptRole: Speaks the entire ad alone, to the viewer. entries.styleDirective: A hyper-realistic, fully three-dimensional living murti — real skin, real weight in the gold, real steel in the weapons, real silk that hangs heavy. She is composited at commanding, larger-than-human scale into a PHOTOREAL Indian business interior that is never restyled around her: she stands on the actual floor in correct perspective, feet planted, casting a firm, defined contact shadow that matches the room's own light. The room's ambient reads a touch cooler around her while a hot saffron-red rim light picks out her crown, shoulders and the trident's edge, so she is lit into the space rather than pasted onto it. Her lion stands beside her, paws on the same real floor, still and alert.
entries.dialogueRhythm: Each clip is a single decisive statement, delivered without hesitation and without a pause inside it — begun and finished in one unbroken line. No questions anywhere in the ad. The force rises across the ad: clip one is level, the middle clips are firmer, the close is absolute. A hard, clean stop at the end of every clip — no trailing off, no softening tail. She never repeats herself and never qualifies anything she has said.
entries.voiceDirection: A commanding female voice from the chest, steady and full, with a controlled edge of power held back rather than released. Slow and measured so the authority reads as certainty and never as anger; consonants clean and firm, sentence ends dropping to a full stop. Volume is strong and constant — no shouting, no shrillness, no growl, no snarl, no rising fury. One and only one change in the whole ad: the final blessing line drops in volume and warms, a mother's voice under the commander's. A tight natural stone-hall tail, no processed reverb, no pitch effects.
entries.expressionDirection: Calm, absolute and unsmiling for almost the entire ad — a face of protection, not of rage. Brows level and relaxed, jaw set, mouth closed and even between lines, no flaring nostrils, no bared teeth, no scowl. The face does not react to anything she says; the certainty never wavers. It changes exactly once, at the very end: on the closing blessing the jaw releases and the mouth softens into a small maternal smile that reaches the eyes, held for the last two seconds. That single change is the whole emotional arc, so nothing before it may anticipate it.
entries.eyeDirection: Level, unblinking and straight into the lens for nearly the whole ad — she does not look away when she names the danger, and she does not look away when she promises. Her head does not turn to follow anything. A single slow, complete blink is permitted, placed just after the promise lands, and no other blink. The third eye stays closed and calm and never opens, never glows. Never a sideways glance, never a look down, never eyes narrowed in anger, never a glowing or white-eyed effect.
entries.gestureDirection: The weapons are HELD, never used. The trishula stands upright and dead still in her upper right hand; the chakra, shankha, sword, bow, arrow and lotus are each held steady in their own hands and none of them moves, swings, spins or is raised. One free hand comes forward into abhaya mudra (palm out, fingers up, at chest level) on the protection line — it arrives in one clean movement and then locks like a seal pressed down, held for the rest of the clip. She never touches, holds or presents the client's products, and never handles money, a phone or a card machine.

entries.label: Lord Shiva

speakers.name: Shiva
speakers.voice: very deep, quiet and slow, with immense stillness behind it
speakers.persona: The ascetic in whom enormous power sits perfectly at rest. He has nothing to prove and nothing to hurry for, so he says the fewest words of anyone and means all of them. speakers.scriptRole: Speaks the entire ad alone, to the viewer. Clip 1 he states one plain truth about the work — what lasts, what does not, what honest work is worth. He never states a price, never speaks digits or a phone number, never raises his voice, and never uses more words than he needs.

entries.styleDirective: A hyper-realistic, fully three-dimensional living murti — real ash-dusted skin with true texture, matted hair with real strand detail, rudraksha with real grain, tiger skin with real fur. No pause inside the line itself: it is spoken as one unbroken, level thought. No questions, no emphasis, no build across the ad — clip five is delivered exactly as calmly as clip one.
entries.voiceDirection: A very deep male voice, beginning each line almost at a whisper and expanding into full resonance by its middle, then settling back down. Very slow — the slowest read in the family — with long, unhurried vowels. Volume stays low throughout; the power comes from depth and calm, never from loudness. No emphasis spikes, no rising urgency, no dramatic pause mid-sentence, no chanting, no Om, no mantra. A long natural cave-or-sanctum tail on the voice and nothing more — no processed reverb, no pitch-shifting, no sub-bass rumble effects. entries.expressionDirection: Eyes half-closed in dhyana and a face that is almost entirely motionless for the whole ad — brow smooth, mouth closed and relaxed between lines, no tension in the jaw, no reaction to anything he says. Only the lips move to form the words, and they move minimally. The single change in the entire ad comes on the closing benediction: the faintest softening at the corners of the mouth, barely a smile, held for the last two seconds. Nothing before it may hint at it. The third eye stays closed, smooth and unlit at all times. He never frowns, never widens his eyes, never opens his mouth wide.
entries.eyeDirection: Eyes closed or nearly closed at the opening of the ad. They open slowly to a half-lidded gaze around the middle clip, and fully — still calm, still unhurried — only on the final blessing. When open, they look THROUGH the lens rather than at it: the gaze is level, unfocused on any object, resting somewhere past the camera. One blink at most in the whole ad. Never a darting look, never a glance around the premises, never a sharp focus pull onto the viewer, never a glowing or white-eyed effect.
entries.gestureDirection: Near-total absence of gesture is the direction. The right hand is raised in abhaya mudra (palm forward, fingers up, at shoulder level) from the first frame to the last and does not move at all. The left hand rests palm-up on the knee in jnana-adjacent stillness and does not move. The trishula stands planted upright in the ground beside him, untouched and unmoving, with the damaru tied to it and silent. If any motion at all is used in the ad, it is one single, very slow opening of the blessing palm on the final line — and if in doubt, use none. He never points, never reaches, never touches, holds or presents the client's products, and never handles money, a phone or a card machine.
entries.bodyLanguage: Seated in padmasana on the tiger skin, spine erect, shoulders level and completely at rest, head balanced and still. Absolutely no sway, no weight shift, no shoulder movement, no breathing motion exaggerated for the camera, no lean towards the lens for the whole clip. The only things that move anywhere in frame are his lips, the thin fall of the Ganga from his jata, and the slow coil-shift of the snake at his neck. He never stands, never walks, never dances, never turns.

A young man, not a child and not a baby. Reach for the real Venugopala of the sanctum — never four-armed Vishnu, never the charioteer of the Gita, never a cartoon Krishna.

speakers.name: Krishna
speakers.voice: youthful, bright and musical, with a light playful lilt
speakers.persona: The charming one who already knows the answer and enjoys watching you arrive at it — quick, warm, lightly teasing, and then unexpectedly wise in the same breath. His mischief is affectionate and never at anyone's expense; his wisdom is delivered casually, as if it were obvious. He is the friendliest voice in the family and the only one who smiles through most of the ad.

entries.expressionDirection: An easy, knowing smile that reaches the eyes, present from the first frame. He never smirks, never winks, never laughs open-mouthed, never pulls a comic face, and the delight never tips into silliness.
entries.eyeDirection: Bright, alive and the most mobile eyes in this family, but never restless. He opens with a sideways kataksha glance — eyes to camera from a slightly turned head — on the teasing line, then comes round into full, warm contact with the lens for the truth of the answer and holds it there. On the closing blessing the gaze stays steady on the lens and softens, with one slow blink as the line ends. Once per ad he may let his eyes travel to the real premises around him and back, on the line that names the business. Never a wink, never a leer, never a glance up-and-away, never eyes closed while speaking.
entries.gestureDirection: The flute is held in both hands at the top of every clip and is LOWERED to about waist level before he speaks — he never plays and talks at the same time, and no flute music is heard. On the answer line the right hand lifts in a light, open abhaya mudra at chest level — easy and unforced, not the stamped seal of Durga nor the held mudra of Shiva — and drops naturally after the line. A single small, playful turn of the wrist is allowed on the teasing line and nowhere else. He never touches the peacock feather, never twirls the flute, never points at, holds or presents the client's products, and never handles money, a phone or a card machine.
