entries.label: Custom God (client's chosen deity)
entries.tagline: The deity the client names blesses the business — built to that deity's own form and temperament
entries.franchise: The ONE specific deity the client names, and no other — for example Venkateswara, Hanuman, Ayyappa, Subrahmanya/Murugan, Saraswati, Rama, Sai Baba, Kanaka Durga, Vishnu, Narasimha or the family's own kula daivam. Take the identity from that deity's own canonical South Indian temple form and devotional calendar art: the tech member writes the named deity's fixed emblems, vahana, number of arms, colours and dress into the prompt ONCE, at the top of the job, and repeats that same list verbatim in every clip so the form cannot drift. If the client's deity already has an entry in this family, use that entry instead of this one. If the canonical form is uncertain, use the most widely worshipped South Indian temple form of that deity and keep it identical in every clip.

speakers.name: Chosen Deity
speakers.voice: calm, resonant and divine, matched to the named deity's own temperament
speakers.persona: Set from the deity the client names, and stated explicitly before anything is generated. Fierce and protective forms (Narasimha, Kali, Bhairava) are certain and immovable; guardian-servant forms (Hanuman, Ayyappa) are devoted, strong and plain-spoken; maternal and serene forms (Saraswati, Annapurna, Parvati) are calm, giving and unhurried; royal forms (Venkateswara, Rama) are gracious, dignified and generous; youthful forms (Murugan) are bright, clear and decisive. Whichever is chosen, it is written down first and then held identically across every clip.
speakers.scriptRole: Speaks the entire ad alone, to the viewer, in three beats taken from the named deity's own domain — Hanuman gives strength and service, Saraswati gives skill and learning, Venkateswara gives fortune and refuge, Narasimha gives protection. Clip 1 names the need that deity answers; each middle clip gives ONE real thing this business offers as that need met; the final clip blesses the business and its family and carries the invitation to come. The deity never states a price, never speaks digits or a phone number, and never endorses or guarantees a product.

entries.styleDirective: A hyper-realistic, fully three-dimensional living murti of the named deity — real skin, real weight in the ornaments, real cloth under gravity. Never a flat calendar print, never a plastic 3D render, never a cartoon. The deity is composited at larger-than-human scale into a PHOTOREAL Indian business interior that is never restyled: standing or seated as that deity's canonical form requires, contacting the actual floor, seat, lotus or vahana in correct perspective, with a soft contact shadow that matches the room's own light. The divine glow takes its COLOUR from the deity named — warm amber and gold for benevolent and royal forms, saffron-red with a hot rim for fierce and guardian forms, cool silver-blue for ascetic forms, clean white-gold for forms of learning and purity — and it must land believably on the real fixtures nearest the figure. Decide the palette once at the top of the job and never change it between clips.
entries.dialogueRhythm: Set to the named deity's temperament and then held for the whole ad. Fierce and guardian forms: one decisive statement per clip, no questions, a hard clean stop. Serene and maternal forms: one flowing thought per clip, ending on a rising, giving note. Royal forms: a measured, gracious two-part line — the recognition, then the boon. Youthful forms: a brisk, bright line with a clear turn in the middle. Whichever is chosen, the pace, the pause length and the stopping style must be identical in every clip, and the last word of each clip is allowed to rest before the cut.
entries.voiceDirection: Cast the voice from the named deity before writing a word, and state it in the prompt: fierce forms get a deep, chest-strong, absolutely steady male voice with the power held back and never released as shouting; guardian-servant forms a strong, plain, devoted male voice with no ornament; maternal and learning forms a clear, serene female voice with even volume and long smooth vowels; royal forms a warm, gracious, unhurried baritone; youthful forms a bright, clean, decisive young voice. In every case the read is slower than a commercial read, the volume is even with no emphasis spikes, and the only processing is a small natural stone-hall tail. Never a narrator, never a dubbing accent, never chanting, never a mantra, never a whispered horror tone, never a comic voice.
entries.expressionDirection: Write the deity's resting face first — the one it holds for most of the ad — and then allow exactly ONE change, placed on the closing blessing. Benevolent and royal forms rest in a settled half-smile and warm by a few millimetres at the end; fierce and guardian forms rest calm, level and unsmiling, protection not rage, and soften into the faintest smile only on the last line; ascetic forms rest almost motionless with half-closed eyes and barely change at all; forms of learning rest in serene composure and brighten minutely at the end. No open-mouthed laughter, no comic faces, no anger, no fear, no surprise, no expression that contradicts the deity's own iconography, and no change that is not written down in advance.
entries.eyeDirection: Reverent and direct as a rule: the gaze meets the lens on every blessing line and does not break mid-sentence, with slow, complete, infrequent blinks. Fierce and guardian forms hold a level, near-unblinking gaze straight into the lens throughout. Maternal and serene forms use the murti gaze — eyes half-lowered, meeting the devotee slightly from above, lids lowering slowly at each sentence end. Ascetic forms keep the eyes half-closed and open them only for the final blessing. Youthful forms may let the eyes travel once to the premises and back. Never darting eyes, never a wink, never a sideways leer, never glowing or white-eyed effects, never eyes closed while a line is spoken unless the ascetic direction calls for it.
entries.gestureDirection: One completed gesture per clip, made slowly and then HELD — hands never punctuate speech. The blessing hand is the deity's own: abhaya mudra (palm forward, fingers up) for protective and reassuring forms, varada mudra (open palm angled down) for giving forms, the deity's own canonical hand sign for forms that have one — Venkateswara's varada and kati hasta, Saraswati's veena and japa mala, Hanuman's folded palms or raised right hand. Every emblem the deity carries — weapon, conch, discus, mace, book, veena, mountain — is held steady, upright and unused: never swung, spun, played or raised at camera. The deity never points at, touches, holds or presents the client's products, and never handles money, a phone or a card machine.
entries.bodyLanguage: Take the posture from the canonical form and then keep the body still — divinity reads as stillness in every entry of this family. Standing forms are planted, weight even, spine straight, shoulders level and squared, with no sway, step or turn. Seated forms sit erect in padmasana or lalitasana with the supporting foot or seat contacting the real floor and no shifting at all. Forms with a vahana keep it still and calm beside or beneath them — it never roars, lunges, moves or interacts with the premises. At most one small settling of the shoulders on the blessing line, and nothing else. No walking, no dancing, no flying, no leaning towards the lens, no crouching, and never sitting on the client's furniture.
entries.cameraDirection: Reverent low angle in all cases — the camera sits at chest level, just below the deity's eye line, and NEVER looks down at a deity from above. Then match the move to the temperament: fierce and guardian forms get a low, wide hero frame and one slow push that locks hard and holds dead still; maternal, giving and royal forms get a slow rise from the feet or lotus to a chest-up frame that then holds; ascetic forms get a locked-off symmetrical wide with an almost imperceptible push; youthful forms get a gentle twenty-to-thirty degree arc that settles frontal. Choose one and use it consistently across the ad. No handheld shake, no whip pan, no crash zoom, no full orbit, no slow-motion, no drone move.
entries.backgroundDirection: The client's own photographs always win — these settings are only for frames that must be generated. With no photos, build the real premises of the client's own trade and dress the frame from THAT deity's tradition, never a generic temple: Venkateswara gets the gold-and-vermilion of a Tirumala-style sanctum with tulasi and a lit deepam; Hanuman gets sindoor-orange stone, a garland of vada and a still oil lamp; Saraswati gets white and pale gold with a lotus pond, palm-leaf books and clean morning light; Murugan gets hill-temple green with peacock-teal and vel-bright steel; Narasimha gets deep shadow, firelight and hot rim light. Pick the palette and the props once at the top of the job and repeat them identically in every clip. Keep the real trade unmistakable — real stock, real counters, real wear — and never let the shrine replace the business.
entries.scriptStyle: Written as a blessing in the register of the deity named, not a pitch. First person, spoken directly to the viewer and the owner, in complete sentences of eight to thirteen spoken words. Take the vocabulary from the deity's own domain — strength and service for Hanuman, refuge and fortune for Venkateswara, learning and skill for Saraswati, protection for the fierce forms — but keep the sentences SPOKEN and everyday: never scriptural, never chanted, never a stotram, never a mantra, never a shloka quotation. The business's real name is said once, with respect. Each middle clip carries one true, specific thing the business actually offers; the deity never guarantees or personally endorses a product, never compares this business to another, and never promises a religious outcome in exchange for a purchase — the deity blesses the effort and the people, and the ad states the facts. The close is a benediction that doubles as the invitation to come.
negatives: Never blend two deities — one named deity only, with only its own emblems, vahana, colours and dress; no borrowed trident, flute, elephant head, chakra, peacock feather, modaka bowl or third eye from any other god
Never substitute a different deity from the one the client named, and never change which deity appears between clips
The named deity's canonical number of arms is fixed for the whole ad — write it down once and keep it identical in every clip, never adding or dropping a pair
Never depict a living human being, guru, saint, politician, film star or the client's own family member as a deity
Never a fantasy, superhero, video-game, anime, cosplay or costume-drama treatment, and never a human actor dressed up as the deity
Never a comic, cute, chibi, cartoon, mascot or meme version — no winking, no thumbs-up, no selfie, no dancing, no modern props
No romanticised, sensual, glamorised or fashion-model treatment; no altered or revealing clothing
No other deity, no priest, no worshipper, no crowd and no human figure anywhere in frame
The deity never holds, touches, points at or presents the client's products, and never handles cash, a card machine or a phone
No violence, no blood, no weapon in use, no demon, no glowing eyes, no lightning, no fire bursts, no lens flare, no CGI energy or sparkle effects
Never a flat poster print, a plastic 3D render, a game cinematic, or a temple photograph pasted behind the figure
No on-screen text, captions, subtitles, logos-as-text, or watermarks
No floating subject — the deity must contact the ground, seat, lotus or vahana with matching shadows
No morphing, no extra or missing limbs, no distorted faces
No background music — clean studio voice only

entries.label: Doraemon (Solo)
entries.tagline: Doraemon alone in the client's shop, presenting the business the way he presents a gadget
entries.franchise: the Japanese anime television series "Doraemon" — the 22nd-century robot cat, exactly as he appears on screen in that show

speakers.name: Doraemon
speakers.voice: bright, round and helpful, with a small proud lift on every reveal
speakers.persona: endlessly helpful and quietly boastful about what he can produce; patient with someone slow to understand, delighted when a hard problem turns out to be easy, and always explains before he shows
speakers.scriptRole: He is the demonstrator. In every clip he names a problem the customer really has, pauses as though reaching for a gadget, and then presents the client's business as the thing that already solves it. He never jokes at the business's expense, and he delivers the closing invitation himself.

entries.styleDirective: One 2D anime-cel character composited into a PHOTOREAL live-action Indian business interior. Doraemon stays flat cel-shaded with clean ink lines; the shop stays photographic and is never restyled, softened or anime-fied. He stands on the real floor at his own true scale relative to the real counters — never resized to fill the frame — with a soft contact shadow that matches the shop's own overhead tube light.
entries.dialogueRhythm: One character, so the CAMERA is his listener. He talks straight down the lens as if the viewer walked in beside him. Each clip is one complete beat: he states the viewer's problem in the first half, then turns his body to the real thing behind him and presents it in the second half — problem, turn, reveal. He never narrates what he is doing; the turn does that. His pause lands exactly where a gadget would be produced, and what emerges is always the shop's real fixture, stock or counter, never a prop.
entries.voiceDirection: Warm mid-register with a childlike round timbre, steady at roughly three words per second. Lift the pitch on the last two words of every reveal and let it fall flat again on the next problem statement, so each clip audibly rises. One clean breath before each reveal — never a gasp. Close-mic and dry: no echo, no processing, no whisper.
entries.expressionDirection: Opens each clip with concerned, brow-raised sympathy while the problem is spoken; the eyes narrow into a knowing smile for exactly the length of the pause; then a wide, open-mouthed proud grin arrives on the reveal and holds to the end of the clip. The grin must never appear early — a smiling face during the problem line kills the beat.
entries.eyeDirection: Locked to the lens through the problem line. One deliberate glance to the real product or counter at the moment of the turn, then straight back to the lens for the reveal and held there. Blink once, on the turn only. No wandering gaze, no half-lidded looks, no drifting to the frame edge.
entries.gestureDirection: Both hands stay low and open while he states the problem. On the pause, one hand goes to his front pouch and stays there — held, not frantically searching. On the reveal the same hand sweeps out flat, palm up, towards the real fixture and stops dead, holding for the rest of the line. One completed gesture per clip; no fluttering.
entries.bodyLanguage: Feet planted, weight even, upright and small-shouldered at rest. The turn is a quarter-rotation from the hips towards the product and back — never a full step off his mark. A slight forward lean of the torso on the closing invitation. He does not bounce, pace or hop between beats.
entries.cameraDirection: Eye level with HIM, not with an adult — the lens sits low so the shop rises behind him. Clip 1: static medium-wide, 35mm feel, full figure with the entrance readable. Middle clips: a slow six-second push-in to a medium as he turns, ending with the real product sharp in the same plane as his hand. Final clip: locked off and slightly wider, no movement at all, so the invitation lands still.
entries.backgroundDirection: With no client photo supplied, generate an ordinary, well-run Indian shop interior of the client's trade — daylight through a glass shopfront on the left mixed with warm ceiling tubes, honest clutter, stocked shelves, a used counter with a card machine. Nothing futuristic, nothing Japanese, nothing sci-fi: the whole charm is a 22nd-century robot standing in a very present-day shop.
entries.scriptStyle: Written as friendly demonstration, not salesmanship. Short declarative sentences in everyday spoken Telugu, one idea per clip. He names the business early and repeats the ONE thing it does best instead of listing everything. Gadget language may frame a line — "this is better than anything in my pocket" — but no invented gadget names, and never a gadget that solves the problem in place of the business. The final clip ends with a clear instruction to come in.
negatives: No Nobita, Shizuka, Gian, Suneo, Dorami or any second character anywhere in frame — this is a solo ad
No invented gadgets, glowing props, sci-fi objects, flying, hovering or time-travel effects — the only thing revealed is the client's real product or premises
No Japanese signage, cherry blossoms or Tokyo street dressing in the environment
Do NOT restyle the shop into anime — the location stays photoreal
Do NOT redraw, re-proportion or re-colour Doraemon — the real television character, identical in every clip
No on-screen text, captions, subtitles, logos-as-text, or watermarks
No floating subject — he must contact the ground with a matching shadow
No morphing, no extra or missing limbs, no distorted faces
No background music — clean studio voice only

entries.label: Shinchan (Solo)
entries.tagline: Shinchan loose in the client's shop, teasing the viewer into walking in
entries.franchise: the Japanese anime television series "Crayon Shin-chan", known in India simply as "Shinchan" — the five-year-old boy exactly as he appears on screen in that show

speakers.name: Shinchan
speakers.voice: cheeky, nasal and sing-song, with a sly flat drop on the punchline
speakers.persona: five years old and completely unbothered; confident far beyond his size, deadpan one second and grinning the next, says the thing an adult would not, adores anything tasty or shiny — never mean, always pleased with himself
speakers.scriptRole: He is the mischief-maker who accidentally sells. Each clip he says something cheeky about the viewer's own excuse for not coming, then names what the business actually does as if he discovered it himself. He takes the credit and gives the business the compliment, and he closes by ordering the viewer to go.

entries.styleDirective: One 2D anime-cel character composited into a PHOTOREAL Indian business interior, staged as if a camera crew followed a small child into a real shop. Shinchan stays cel-drawn with flat colour; the shop keeps its photographic grain, reflections and imperfections. He holds his own true scale from the show against real adult-height counters and doorways — never enlarged to match the frame — and his contact shadow falls in the same direction as every real shadow in the photograph.
entries.dialogueRhythm: One character, and the camera is the adult he is teasing. Each clip he opens facing AWAY — talking at a shelf, a counter or an off-screen shopkeeper — then whips round to the lens and tells the viewer the real point like it is a secret. Away-shot for the set-up, straight to camera for the pay-off, every single clip. Half the comedy is the pause before he turns. The pay-off is always about the business, never about himself, and no two clips use the same joke structure.
entries.voiceDirection: Bright, slightly nasal child register with a sing-song lilt on the set-up and a flat deadpan drop on the pay-off — the drop is the joke. Faster than natural, about four words per second, then a full half-second of silence before the turn. Never shout, never squeal: cheek reads as confidence, not volume. Dry close-mic, no room tone, no effects.
entries.expressionDirection: Blank, unimpressed, half-lidded deadpan through the set-up, held a beat longer than is comfortable. On the turn the eyes widen and a closed-mouth smirk arrives first, opening into a full toothy grin by the last word. The eyebrows carry it: flat on the set-up, one raised on the turn, both up on the pay-off. Never grin during the set-up.
entries.eyeDirection: Off-camera and slightly downward through the set-up, as though inspecting something at his own eye level. On the turn the eyes snap to the lens in one move and lock there without blinking for the whole pay-off. One slow blink after the final word, then hold. He never looks at camera and away again mid-line.
entries.gestureDirection: Hands behind his back or hanging loose during the set-up — no gesturing while deadpan. On the pay-off one hand comes up in a single confident move: a thumb jerked at the real product behind him, a flat palm presenting it, or one finger raised as if he has just decided something. It stays up until the line ends. Never both hands, never waving.
entries.bodyLanguage: Weight on one leg, hip cocked, relaxed to the point of rudeness, rocking on his heels through the set-up. The turn is a full-body pivot — shoulders first, feet following — landing square to camera. A slight lean towards the lens on the closing invitation, as if letting the viewer in on it. No running, no dancing, no jumping.
entries.cameraDirection: Handheld at HIS eye level with a wide 24mm feel, so the shop looms and he owns the foreground, carrying a live but gentle sway. Clip 1: static through the set-up, then a quick reframe as he turns, landing him slightly off-centre. Middle clips: a slow sideways drift past a real shelf that keeps him at the frame edge until the turn brings him to centre. Final clip: the sway stops and settles to a clean waist-up for the invitation.
entries.backgroundDirection: Late-afternoon five o'clock light coming in low through the shop door, warm on one side and cool tube light on the other. A genuinely busy, lived-in shop: stock out of its boxes, a stool, a mat, a wall calendar, real wear on the counter edge. Adults implied but never seen — a hand-cart outside, chappals by the door. Nothing in Japan, no house interior, no kindergarten.
entries.scriptStyle: Written as a child's cheeky commentary in the plainest spoken Telugu of the whole family — short blunt sentences, no stacked adjectives, no slogan words. The set-up may tease the VIEWER (their delay, their excuse, their doubt) and must never tease the client, the staff or the price. One catchphrase-style flourish in the entire ad, no more. The close is Shinchan telling the viewer to come, phrased as an instruction he fully expects to be obeyed.
negatives: None of the show's rude gags — no bare-bottom dance, no removing clothes, no elephant joke, no toilet humour of any kind; this is a family business ad
No Misae, Hiroshi, Himawari, Shiro or any second character in frame
No mocking the client, the staff, the price or the premises — the tease is aimed only at the viewer
No Japanese house, school or street dressing in the environment
Do NOT restyle the shop into anime — the location stays photoreal
Do NOT redraw or re-proportion Shinchan — the real television character, identical in every clip
No on-screen text, captions, subtitles, logos-as-text, or watermarks
No floating subject — he must contact the ground with a matching shadow
No morphing, no extra or missing limbs, no distorted faces
No background music — clean studio voice only

entries.label: Chhota Bheem (Solo)
entries.tagline: Bheem tests the client's business himself and puts his word behind it
entries.franchise: the Indian animated television series "Chhota Bheem" — Bheem exactly as he appears on screen in that show

speakers.name: Chhota Bheem
speakers.voice: clear, strong and open-chested, with a confident settled finish
speakers.persona: brave and straightforward, protective of ordinary people, with no arrogance and no cunning; he states things plainly, praises honestly, and backs a claim by testing it himself
speakers.scriptRole: He is the guarantor. Each clip he raises a doubt a real customer would have, tests or inspects the real thing on camera, and gives a plain verdict. His word is the proof, so he never exaggerates, and he closes by telling the viewer he stands behind this place.

entries.styleDirective: One Indian television cartoon character composited into a PHOTOREAL working business — flat, hand-animated and unmodified against a photograph that stays photographic. Bheem holds his own scale from the show against real doorways, sacks and shelving and is never scaled up into a giant. His weight shows in the contact shadow: dense directly beneath his feet, softening outward.
entries.dialogueRhythm: One character with nobody to answer him, so the OBJECT answers. Each clip runs doubt, action, verdict: he speaks the doubt to camera, physically engages the real thing — lifts it, opens it, presses it, checks it — through a beat of silence, then delivers the verdict to camera. The silent middle beat is mandatory; it is what makes the verdict worth anything. He addresses the viewer the way he addresses the people of Dholakpur: as a crowd he feels responsible for, plural and direct.
entries.voiceDirection: Chest-resonant and unhurried at roughly two and a half words per second, landing every consonant. Volume stays level — he never shouts, because certainty is quiet. Drop the pitch a step on the verdict and hold the final word half a beat longer than natural. A full breath before each clip's first word so the line arrives on support.
entries.expressionDirection: Level, serious brow while the doubt is spoken — no smile at all. Through the silent test the face concentrates: eyes narrowed, jaw set. On the verdict the brow releases and an approving closed-mouth smile arrives, widening only for the final clip's invitation. The smile is earned once per clip and never precedes the test.
entries.eyeDirection: Straight to lens for the doubt, unblinking. Down to his own hands and the real object throughout the test, honestly following what he is doing. Back up to the lens on the verdict with one decisive blink at the moment the eyes return. He never glances away while speaking.
entries.gestureDirection: Arms at rest, hands open and relaxed during the doubt. The test uses both hands with real intent — gripping a handle, lifting a sack, pressing a surface, turning a product over — and the effort shows in the fingers. On the verdict one hand rests flat on the tested object, or a single open palm turns towards it. No pointing, no flourish, no folded arms.
entries.bodyLanguage: Stance wide and grounded, shoulders back, spine tall. He moves his whole body to reach, bending from the knees rather than the waist, and returns to the identical planted stance for every verdict. On the close he squares fully to camera, feet apart, and holds completely still. No fighting poses, no flexing, no leaping.
entries.cameraDirection: Low, at chest level looking slightly up, so he reads as the most solid thing in the room. Clip 1: a slow eight-second arc from three-quarter to frontal, the shop revolving behind him. Middle clips: locked off in a medium for the doubt, a small push to a tight two-hand insert on the test, then back out to the medium for the verdict. Final clip: static and symmetrical, wide enough to show the whole premises around him.
entries.backgroundDirection: Mid-morning, full daylight, shutters up and the frontage wide open. Choose the substantial part of the business — stacked sacks, cylinders, crates, heavy shelving, machinery, a loading corner — anything with real mass he can plausibly test. High ceiling where the trade allows, deep aisles, dust visible in the light beam. A present-day Indian working premises: never a village set, never a fort, never a mud-hut street.
entries.scriptStyle: Plain declarative Telugu in a slightly formal, respectful register — the way a trusted elder brother speaks to a village. Short sentences, concrete nouns, no wordplay, no boasting. Every claim must be one the shopkeeper could actually stand behind. Strength language is allowed only as a metaphor for reliability, never as a stunt. The close is a personal assurance followed by a clear instruction to visit.
negatives: No Chutki, Raju, Jaggu, Kalia, Dholu-Bholu or any second character in frame — this is a solo ad
No laddoos, no strength-boost transformation, no glow effects, no flying leaps or superhuman feats — his strength is only ever ordinary lifting
No fighting, no villains, no weapons anywhere in frame
No Dholakpur village dressing, forts, mud huts or period styling in the environment — this is a present-day Indian business
Do NOT restyle the premises into a cartoon — the location stays photoreal
Do NOT redraw or re-proportion Bheem — the real television character, identical in every clip
No on-screen text, captions, subtitles, logos-as-text, or watermarks

No morphing, no extra or missing limbs, no distorted faces

entries.label: Mickey Mouse (Solo)
entries.tagline: Mickey walks the viewer through the client's business as its personal host
entries.franchise: the classic Walt Disney animated cartoons — Mickey Mouse exactly as he appears in the original shorts

speakers.name: Mickey Mouse
speakers.voice: high, bright and welcoming, with a lilting musical warmth
speakers.persona: the gracious host — cheerful, courteous, endlessly optimistic, delighted by small things and quick to compliment; never sarcastic and never funny at anyone's expense
speakers.scriptRole: He is the tour guide. Each clip he welcomes the viewer into one more part of the business, points out what makes it special, and hands the compliment to the owner rather than to himself. He opens the ad with a greeting and closes it holding the door open.

entries.styleDirective: One classic Disney 2D cartoon character composited into a PHOTOREAL Indian business, drawn with the clean rubber-hose line and flat colour of the original shorts while the shop keeps every photographic reflection, scratch and speck of dust. He stays at his own true scale beside the real counters, never resized, and casts a soft-edged contact shadow that agrees with the shop's own key light.
entries.dialogueRhythm: One character carrying a walking tour. He is always moving and always speaking to the lens, which he treats as a guest he personally invited. Each clip begins mid-stride with a welcome or an "and look at this", arrives at one real feature, and ends with him stopping, turning fully to camera and making the point. Movement, arrival, point — three beats, every clip. The camera walking beside him replaces the second character, and he glances back to check the viewer is keeping up.
entries.voiceDirection: High, light and forward, with a musical rise and fall — every sentence lifts in the middle and settles at the end. Brisk but never rushed, around three and a half words per second, with an audible smile through the entire read. A small delighted intake of breath before each new feature. At most one cheerful exclamation in the whole ad, and no giggling under the lines.
entries.expressionDirection: Permanently pleased, but graded: an open welcoming smile while walking, eyebrows lifting into genuine delight at the moment of arrival, and the widest smile of the clip saved for the turn to camera. On the closing invitation the expression shifts from excited to sincere — a smaller smile, warmer eyes. Never a neutral or bored beat.
entries.eyeDirection: On the lens while walking, as if keeping up a conversation with a guest at his side. Away to the real feature at the moment of arrival, unhurried, so the viewer's eye follows his. Then back to the lens and held. On the close, a slow blink and steady unbroken contact through the final three words.
entries.gestureDirection: Open presentational hands throughout — palms up, fingers relaxed, arms swinging from the shoulder in wide unhurried arcs. Exactly one big two-handed presentation in the whole ad, saved for the strongest feature; elsewhere a single hand indicates. On the close one arm extends towards the entrance and holds, inviting the viewer through it.
entries.bodyLanguage: A light bouncing walk with a lift on each step, torso upright, shoulders loose. He leads with the shoulder nearest camera and turns his whole body to face the lens at each stop — never just the head. Weight settles onto both feet at every arrival. No skipping, no dancing, no slapstick stumbles.
entries.cameraDirection: A smooth lateral steadicam that walks with him at his own eye level, 40mm feel, holding him a third into frame with the business unspooling behind. Clip 1: track in from the entrance beside him. Middle clips: the track slows and stops as he arrives, letting him settle into a medium. Final clip: the camera stops entirely and he walks back towards it, ending on a warm medium-close with the doorway light behind him.
entries.backgroundDirection: Early evening with all the shop's own lighting on — display lights, showcase glow, a warm lamp at the counter — the most welcoming the premises ever looks. Tidy, freshly arranged, nothing under repair. Give him a walkable path: an aisle, a corridor of shelves, or a counter run he can move along. No theme park, no castle, no American storefront.
entries.scriptStyle: Written as gracious hosting: warm, courteous Telugu in the second person throughout — "you will see", "come and look". Every clip carries one compliment aimed at the business or the people who run it, never at Mickey. No sarcasm, no comparison to competitors, no stacked exclamations. The close is an invitation, phrased as a door being held open.

Clip 1: an over-the-shoulder from behind, his back to us and the shop ahead — we are with him, not looking at him. Middle clips: a slow six-second arc from three-quarter-back to profile as he straightens, 50mm at eye level. Final clip: fully frontal, static, medium-close, the business clean behind him. The camera's journey around him mirrors his change of mind.
entries.backgroundDirection: Begin at the threshold — the entrance seen as a customer arriving sees it, overcast street light outside and warm shop light inside, so stepping in reads as relief. Middle clips move deeper into the premises to where the solution physically lives: the counter, the service desk, the price board. Ordinary, honest, mid-afternoon. No Japanese house, no classroom, no school corridor, no Tokyo street.
entries.scriptStyle: Written as overheard muttering in the most ordinary spoken Telugu of the whole family — sentences that sound thrown away but are grammatically whole, filler words allowed, and no advertising vocabulary at all. Each clip names one genuine customer excuse (put it off, assumed it was expensive, went somewhere cheaper, did not know it existed) and lets the business answer it without being praised. The close is a plain admission followed by a plain recommendation.

entries.label: SpongeBob (Solo)
entries.tagline: SpongeBob works the client's shop like it is the best job in the world
entries.franchise: the American animated television series "SpongeBob SquarePants" — SpongeBob exactly as he appears on screen in that show

speakers.name: SpongeBob
speakers.voice: bright, nasal and irrepressibly cheerful, cracking upward on the biggest word
speakers.persona: sincerely, exhaustingly enthusiastic; he treats work as the finest thing in the world, finds genuine wonder in ordinary objects, takes every product completely seriously, and has never had a cynical thought
speakers.scriptRole: He is the world's most enthusiastic employee of a business he does not work at. Each clip he seizes on one ordinary detail of the client's premises and treats it as magnificent — and because the detail is real, the praise lands. He does the work on camera, and closes by telling the viewer they have to see this for themselves.

entries.styleDirective: One American 2D television cartoon character composited into a PHOTOREAL Indian business — flat, saturated and hard-lined against a photograph that stays photographic and DRY. He holds his own true scale from the show against real counters and shelves, never enlarged, and contacts the floor with a crisp shadow. Nothing in the environment becomes underwater, wobbly or cartoonish.
entries.dialogueRhythm: One character at maximum energy, carried by DOING rather than presenting. Each clip he is already mid-task when we arrive — wiping a counter, straightening stock, holding a product up to the light — talks to the lens without stopping the task, and finishes on a triumphant flourish with the real object in hand. Task, talk, flourish. Because he never pauses, the ad's variety comes from changing task and zone every clip, never from changing his mood. His energy stays at ten throughout; only the last clip drops to a sincere eight for the invitation.
entries.voiceDirection: High, nasal, forward and fast — around four words per second, the quickest read in this family — with a genuine upward crack on the single biggest word of each clip. Full-throated but never shouted into the mic; keep it clean and dry. One short delighted laugh is allowed, in the middle of the ad and never at the end. Final clip: same voice, twenty percent slower and warmer, so sincerity closes the ad.
entries.expressionDirection: An enormous open-mouthed grin from the first frame, eyes squeezed happy. On the key word the eyes fly wide open and the grin somehow widens — that is the beat the clip is built around. Between beats he wears an earnest, focused work-face with the tongue slightly out in concentration, which makes the return to the grin funny. Never neutral, never tired, never sad.
entries.eyeDirection: Locked on his task with total sincerity while working, then up to the lens in one snap for the talk, holding there through the whole line. At the flourish he looks at the real object first and back at the lens for the final word. Blinks are big and infrequent. He never looks bored at what he is holding — the product always receives an admiring look.
entries.gestureDirection: Constant purposeful hand activity — he is always holding something real: a cloth, a packet, a tool of the trade. Both hands stay busy through the talk. The flourish is one big two-handed lift of the real product towards camera, held high and completely still for a beat, the only time in the clip his hands stop. No flailing, no jazz hands, no gesture that drops the object.
entries.bodyLanguage: Springy and upright, in constant small motion — bouncing on the spot, rocking with the scrub, leaning eagerly across the counter. He works with his whole body. On the flourish he plants both feet, straightens fully and freezes, and that sudden stillness is what sells it. On the close he stands square with his hands at his sides, still for the first time in the ad. No spinning, no cartwheels.
entries.cameraDirection: Wide 24mm from slightly low, close enough that the energy fills the frame. Clip 1: a fast push-in on him mid-task, arriving as he looks up. Middle clips: a quick decisive whip-pan or snap-zoom landing on the flourish — this is the only entry in this family that uses aggressive camera moves. Final clip: everything stops — locked-off medium, no push, no zoom — so the sincere close reads as a change of gear.
entries.backgroundDirection: The brightest, cleanest, most colourful part of the business at high noon: full high-key light, no moody shadow, saturated real stock, a spotless counter. Choose a zone where a task is plausible — a service counter, a preparation area, a display being arranged. Everything DRY and Indian: no water, no bubbles, no aquatic props, no Bikini Bottom, no pineapple, no American diner.
entries.scriptStyle: Written as sincere over-enthusiasm: short, high-energy Telugu sentences with one superlative per clip and never two, always attached to a real specific detail of the business rather than a vague claim. He praises the work and the people, never the price alone. No catchphrases, no laughter written into the script, no nonsense words. The close drops the volume and becomes a genuine personal recommendation.

entries.label: Oggy (Solo)
entries.tagline: Oggy inspects the client's premises in silence and finds nothing to complain about
entries.franchise: the French animated television series "Oggy and the Cockroaches" — Oggy exactly as he appears on screen in that show

speakers.name: Oggy
speakers.voice: an unseen narrator's smooth, gently ironic, well-mannered tone — Oggy himself never speaks
speakers.persona: house-proud and long-suffering: he wants everything clean, ordered and calm, takes visible pleasure in a tidy surface, and braces for disaster out of pure habit even when none arrives; gentle, fussy and quietly satisfied, communicating only in sighs, gasps and small hums
speakers.scriptRole: He is the standard, played silently. The narrator carries every word while Oggy inspects the client's premises the way he inspects his own home — running a finger along a surface, straightening a row, checking a corner — and finds nothing to fix. His visible relief IS the endorsement, and the ad closes on him finally sitting down, content.

entries.styleDirective: One French 2D television cartoon character composited into a PHOTOREAL Indian business — clean flat colour and a bold outline against premises that stay fully photographic and untouched. He keeps his own true scale beside real counters and doorways, never resized, and every place he touches the real world reads: a contact shadow under his feet, and a visible point of contact where his hand meets a shelf or surface.
entries.dialogueRhythm: HE DOES NOT SPEAK — put this at the top of the brief: Oggy is a non-speaking character, so the entire script belongs to an unseen narrator while Oggy performs it in pantomime. Each clip is a silent inspection in three beats: he approaches something with suspicion, checks it carefully, and relaxes because it is genuinely fine. The narrator names the thing being checked as he approaches, states what the business does about it as he checks, and falls silent for the relief beat. The absence of disaster is both the joke and the selling point — in this shop, nothing goes wrong.
entries.voiceDirection: Narrator only: smooth, warm, gently ironic and unhurried at about two and a half words per second, in the register of a well-mannered storyteller who finds the whole thing charming. Always finish the line before the relief beat and let the silence sit for a full second. Oggy contributes at most one non-verbal sound per clip — a small worried hum or a long satisfied sigh — mixed low. He is never lip-synced and never spoken for in the first person.
entries.expressionDirection: Narrow-eyed pursed suspicion on the approach, brows drawn together. Utterly blank and focused during the check — the face gives nothing away, which is what builds the beat. Then the whole face releases at once: brows up, eyes softening, a slow closed-mouth smile and an audible exhale. Suspicion, blankness, relief, in that order, every clip. The relief must never arrive early.
entries.eyeDirection: Slow deliberate sweeps of the environment on the approach — corners first, the way a fussy person really looks at a room. Fixed hard and unblinking on the detail being checked. On relief the eyes lift and soften towards the wider premises. Once per ad, in the final clip only, he looks directly at the lens and holds it with quiet approval.
entries.gestureDirection: One finger drawn along a real surface and then inspected — the signature check, used once and never repeated the same way. Elsewhere: straightening a row of items by a centimetre, tapping a shelf edge, opening and closing something gently. Every touch is light and reverent; he handles the client's things better than the client does. On relief the hands clasp behind his back or fold in front, satisfied.
entries.bodyLanguage: Stiff, tiptoed and tense-shouldered on the approach, moving in small careful steps. He bends at the waist to look closely rather than crouching. At relief the shoulders drop visibly and the walk becomes normal. In the final clip he lowers himself onto a stool or chair in the premises and sits — the first time he sits in the whole ad — and stays there for the close.
entries.cameraDirection: Slow, elegant and patient: a gliding dolly on a 50mm, one continuous move per clip, no handheld anywhere. Clip 1: a lateral glide following him along a counter at walking pace. Middle clips: a slow push from a wide to a tight insert on his hand and the surface, then a gentle pull back to catch the relief on his face. Final clip: the dolly comes to rest and holds a still, wide, symmetrical frame of him seated in a spotless premises.
entries.backgroundDirection: A spotless, freshly cleaned business photographed just after opening — shutters up, floor still gleaming, everything squared away, early low sunlight raking across clean surfaces to make them shine. Emphasise order: aligned stock, wiped glass, a clear counter, tidy corners. It must be a real Indian premises in genuinely good condition, and the sales member should be told this entry only works when the client's place is actually clean.
entries.scriptStyle: Third-person Telugu narration written with quiet, well-mannered irony: measured sentences, one standard checked per clip — cleanliness, freshness, order, care, punctuality — each tied to something the business genuinely does. No dialogue, no written sound effects, no first person for Oggy. Never mention pests, dirt or anything the business could be accused of. The close is the narrator observing that even Oggy found nothing to complain about, and inviting the viewer in.

entries.label: Motu & Patlu
entries.tagline: The safe all-purpose pick — one blurts the doubt every customer has, the other settles it, inside the client's own shop.
entries.franchise: the Indian animated television series "Motu Patlu"

speakers.name: Motu
speakers.voice: high-pitched, bubbly and excitable
speakers.persona: warm-hearted, impulsive, food-loving, easily amazed, asks what everyone is thinking; speaks quickly
speakers.scriptRole: Opens every clip. He asks the customer's real question, reacts with excitement or friendly doubt, and sets up the line that follows. He never delivers the offer or the call to action.

speakers.name: Patlu
speakers.voice: calm, measured, clear and unhurried
speakers.persona: logical, well-informed, patient, quietly witty, the one who always has the answer; speaks slower than Motu
speakers.scriptRole: Answers Motu in every clip. He carries the business value — the service, the offer, the proof — and delivers the closing call to action in the final clip.

entries.styleDirective: 2D cartoon characters composited into a PHOTOREAL live-action environment. The characters stay cartoon; the location stays photographic and is never restyled. They stand on the actual floor in correct perspective, casting soft contact shadows that match the scene's light.
entries.dialogueRhythm: Motu speaks first and sets up the question or reaction; Patlu answers with the business value. This order never reverses. Both characters speak in every single clip. The comic beat is scale: Motu reacts bigger than the moment deserves and Patlu answers smaller than expected, and the gap between the two sizes is the joke.
entries.voiceDirection: Two voices that must never sit at the same pitch: Motu rides high, fast and slightly breathless and lifts on the last word of his question; Patlu answers a full tone lower and noticeably slower, unhurried right to the end of his sentence. Energy climbs across the ad — Motu louder and more delighted each clip, Patlu staying exactly as calm — and the final line is Patlu's warmest, slowest and most direct reading. Clean studio recording, no reverb, no narrator, no third voice.
entries.expressionDirection: Motu opens each clip wide-eyed with both brows up and his mouth open mid-question, and resolves into a full open-mouthed grin the moment Patlu's answer lands. Patlu holds a small, closed-mouth, certain smile throughout with level brows, and raises exactly one brow on the single word that carries the offer or the proof. On the closing clip both faces settle into an easy direct smile at the viewer — Motu's delighted, Patlu's reassuring.
entries.eyeDirection: Motu's gaze bounces: to the real product or fixture he is asking about, up to Patlu, and only on his last two words to the lens. Patlu keeps his eyes on Motu for the whole of his answer — he is talking to his friend, not announcing — and turns to camera only in the final clip, holding the lens steady through the call to action. Neither ever stares blankly past the camera.
entries.gestureDirection: Motu points with a whole open hand at whatever he is asking about, then both hands rise near his chest in disbelief; his hands are always moving while he speaks. Patlu gestures once and only once per clip — a single calm open palm turned towards the real shelf, counter or machine as he names the reason — then lets the hand drop and stay still. On the final line Patlu's open palm turns towards the viewer: an invitation, not a point.
entries.bodyLanguage: Both stand square on the real floor with weight settled, angled about thirty degrees towards each other and open to camera. Motu leans in and rocks forward on his question, sometimes taking a half step towards the thing exciting him; Patlu stays planted and completely still, which is the whole joke — one of them is bouncing and the other has not moved. In the closing frame both turn front-on together, shoulders relaxed, the business wide open behind them.
entries.cameraDirection: Eye-level medium two-shot, lens level matched to the client photograph so the pair sit in the room rather than on it. Compose with the business's working detail — shelves, counter, stock — filling the space between and behind them, both characters fully in frame with clean headroom. Movement is at most one slow push-in across the clip; the comedy is staged inside a held frame and never chased by the camera.
entries.backgroundDirection: With no client photographs, build an ordinary, busy Indian main-road version of this exact business type: real stock stacked the way a working shop stacks it, a scuffed floor, a real billing counter, daylight from the shutter side with warm tube light inside. It must look like a shop that opened this morning and has been trading all day — never a showroom render, never an empty set, and never Furfuri Nagar or any location from the show.
entries.scriptStyle: Plain, everyday spoken Telugu between two friends standing in a shop — the way people actually talk, not the way copy is written. Motu's line is always a question or an exclamation and never states a fact; Patlu's line is always a plain statement that answers the exact thing Motu just asked and carries one real, specific detail from the business information. The humour comes from Motu's appetite and over-reaction, never from a pun and never from a written slogan, and the closing line is Patlu telling the viewer plainly what to do.

entries.label: Doraemon & Nobita
entries.tagline: Gentle and family-safe — the worried one asks, the ordinary one already has the answer, and no gadget is ever needed.
entries.franchise: the Japanese animated television series "Doraemon", in its Shin-Ei Animation television look

speakers.name: Doraemon
speakers.voice: round, friendly and slightly nasal, warm in the middle of the range with a small worried wobble
speakers.persona: caring, fussy, quick to worry on his friend's behalf, easily impressed, reaches for a solution before he has heard the whole problem; speaks in short warm bursts
speakers.scriptRole: Opens every clip. He asks the customer's real question as a worry, and half-reaches for the gadget he is never going to need. He never delivers the offer or the call to action.

speakers.name: Nobita
speakers.voice: light, boyish and thin, brightening upward with excitement and never hurried
speakers.persona: ordinary, honest, usually the one being rescued — and here, for once, the one who already found the answer and is quietly proud of it; simple words, no cleverness
speakers.scriptRole: Answers Doraemon in every clip. For once he is the one who knows: he carries the business value — the service, the offer, the proof — and delivers the closing call to action in the final clip.

entries.styleDirective: Clean cel-animation anime characters, thin even outlines and flat colour exactly as the television series draws them, composited into a PHOTOREAL live-action environment. The characters stay animated; the location stays photographic and is never restyled or given anime lighting. They stand on the actual floor in correct perspective, casting soft contact shadows that match the scene's light.
entries.dialogueRhythm: Doraemon speaks first, worrying at the customer's problem and half-reaching towards his pocket; Nobita answers with the business value and the running joke lands — this shop has already solved it, so the gadget is never needed. The pocket is reached for in every clip and nothing is ever pulled out of it. This order never reverses, and both characters speak in every single clip.
entries.voiceDirection: Doraemon's lines start slightly anxious and land relieved; Nobita's start bright and end certain, so the clip's emotional turn happens between the two voices rather than inside either one. Keep Doraemon rounder and closer to the mic and Nobita thinner and a touch further back, so a listener can tell them apart with their eyes shut. Both stay light and childlike, and the closing line is Nobita's — slower and prouder than anything he has said before. Clean studio recording, no reverb, no narrator.
entries.expressionDirection: Doraemon opens with his brows pushed together, a small worried mouth and wide eyes; the worry breaks into a big open-mouthed relieved smile the instant Nobita answers. Nobita starts with a plain unbothered face and grows a slow pleased grin across his line, his chin lifting slightly by the last word. In the closing clip both drop the comedy and smile straight down the lens — Doraemon round and delighted, Nobita simple and sincere.
entries.eyeDirection: Doraemon's eyes go first to whatever is worrying him in the real premises, then flick down towards his own pocket, then up to Nobita — that three-beat look is the running gag and it happens exactly once per clip. Nobita looks at Doraemon throughout his answer, then turns to camera on the final clip's last words and holds the lens without blinking away. Neither character searches around the frame aimlessly.
entries.gestureDirection: Doraemon's hands are round and flat: one rises to his cheek in worry while the other hovers at his front pocket and stops there — the hand never goes in and nothing is ever produced. Nobita gestures small and specific: a single finger or flat hand indicating the real shelf, counter or machine he is naming, then both hands folded loosely in front of him. On the closing line Nobita's hand opens towards the viewer in a plain come-in gesture.
entries.bodyLanguage: Doraemon stands short, upright and slightly bouncy, rocking back on his heels when he is surprised; Nobita stands loose and a little slouched until his answer, when he straightens and squares his shoulders — for once he is the one holding the room. Keep them close together, almost shoulder to shoulder, the way two friends who walked in together stand. Both plant flat on the real floor with matching contact shadows.
entries.cameraDirection: Frame at the pair's own eye level — a low camera by adult standards — so the room is seen from a child's eye level, which is what makes them read as being inside it. Static medium two-shot for most clips with the real fixtures kept clean and readable behind them; hold the frame and let the performance move. Allow one slow push-in on the proof clip only, and finish the closing clip a touch wider with the whole business visible around them.
entries.backgroundDirection: With no client photographs, build a tidy, human-scale neighbourhood version of this exact business — the kind of small clean premises a child could walk into alone — with real stock, a real counter, soft daylight through the front and even fill inside. Keep it Indian and specific to the client's trade: never a Japanese street, never a tatami room, never Japanese signage, and never the show's own town.
entries.scriptStyle: Simple, warm spoken Telugu at a child's vocabulary — short sentences, no clever words, nothing a ten-year-old would not say. Doraemon's line is always the worry or the question, phrased the way a real customer phrases their doubt; Nobita's line answers it with one concrete thing this business really does, said plainly and proudly. The comedy is the reversal — the ordinary one has the answer and the magic is unnecessary — and it is never explained out loud. The closing line is Nobita's straightforward invitation to come.

entries.label: Tom & Jerry
entries.tagline: Pure pantomime with a storyteller's voice-over — the two never speak, so the comedy is all faces and hands.
entries.franchise: the classic American theatrical cartoon series "Tom and Jerry" (Hanna-Barbera / MGM)

speakers.name: Tom
speakers.voice: narrated, deep, dry and long-suffering — the storyteller's Tom register, with Tom's own mouth never moving
speakers.persona: proud, scheming, easily embarrassed, always certain he has understood and always half a step behind; every feeling arrives on his face before anyone explains it
speakers.scriptRole: Opens every clip, in pantomime. He physically asks the customer's real question — the doubt, the double-take, the disbelief — and the narrator voices that thought for him. He never delivers the offer or the call to action.

speakers.name: Jerry
speakers.voice: narrated, lighter, quicker and amused — the same single storyteller lifting into his Jerry register, with Jerry's own mouth never moving
speakers.persona: small, quick and unbothered, several steps ahead; answers with a shrug and a look rather than an argument, and is never smug for long
speakers.scriptRole: Answers Tom in every clip, in pantomime. He carries the business value — the service, the offer, the proof — shown as much as spoken, and the narrator delivers the closing call to action over his final gesture.

entries.styleDirective: Classic hand-drawn theatrical cartoon characters, full-animation line and shading exactly as the original shorts draw them, composited into a PHOTOREAL live-action environment. The characters stay drawn; the location stays photographic and is never restyled, never aged, and never given a vintage grade or film-frame border. Both make real contact with the surfaces they stand on, in correct perspective, with soft shadows matching the room's light.
entries.dialogueRhythm: Tom and Jerry never speak in the original and they do not speak here: nothing is lip-synced and neither mouth ever forms a word. The entire exchange is carried by ONE narrator's voice-over — a dry register for Tom's part, a lighter one for Jerry's — laid over pure pantomime, so every written line must be a thought that a face and a pair of hands can actually perform. Tom's mime raises the question first and Jerry's answers it; that order never reverses, and both characters perform in every single clip.
entries.voiceDirection: One narrator voices the whole ad and never sounds like a cartoon: a warm dry storyteller who drops half a tone and slows for Tom's part and lifts and quickens for Jerry's, so a listener always knows whose thought it is. He is amused by them and never mocking, and he never announces — he is telling a friend what he just watched. The closing line is his slowest and most direct, spoken over Jerry's invitation. Clean studio recording, no reverb, no second voice actor, no cartoon yowls or squeaks on the track.
entries.expressionDirection: Tom carries the whole first half on his face: a slow blink, brows climbing, jaw dropping open on the question, then a flat deadpan aimed at nothing when Jerry proves him wrong. Jerry answers with one raised brow and a small closed-mouth smirk that softens into a genuine friendly smile by the end of his beat. Both mouths stay shut — no word shapes, no lip-sync — and each change of expression must land exactly on the narrated word it belongs to. In the closing clip both drop the rivalry and give the lens a warm open look.
entries.eyeDirection: Tom's eyes lead every beat: they lock onto the real product or fixture, widen, slide sideways to Jerry, then roll or fall flat when he is beaten — and only in the last clip do they finally meet the lens. Jerry looks up at Tom with steady patient amusement, glances once at the thing that proves the point, and turns to camera a beat before the closing line so the invitation lands on his look. Neither ever stares blankly; here the gaze IS the dialogue.
entries.gestureDirection: Tom mimes big and slow — a flat palm presented at the shelf as if asking "well?", both arms thrown wide in disbelief, one finger raised on a point he never finishes. Jerry mimes small and precise: a casual thumb towards the real thing being discussed, a shrug with both little palms up, and on the final clip an open two-handed "come in" towards the viewer. Every gesture must read with the sound off — if the mime does not work silently, restage it.
entries.bodyLanguage: Tom takes up space: he leans in, straightens up too proudly, then slumps in defeat, all inside one clip, with his weight visibly shifting on the real floor. Jerry stays compact and unhurried, standing on a real surface that exists in the photograph — a counter edge, a step, a stacked box — at a believable height for his size, never floating and never scaled up. Stage them with a clear separation in depth so both read at once, and end the ad with the two side by side, rivalry set down, facing the viewer together.
entries.cameraDirection: Stage it like the shorts: a clean, wide-enough held frame with both characters visible head to foot so the pantomime has room to play. Keep the camera locked for the set-up and, if anything moves at all, allow a single slow push towards Tom on the reaction beat — never a whip, never a cut inside the clip. Match the lens level to the client photograph and compose so Jerry's real perch and Tom's full figure share one readable plane against the business.
entries.backgroundDirection: With no client photographs, build a photoreal, warmly lit Indian premises of exactly this trade with plenty of usable staging furniture — a solid counter, shelving with real stock, a step or crate Jerry can genuinely stand on — because this comedy needs levels. Everything stays real and intact: no mouse holes, no cartoon props, no household-cartoon kitchen, and nothing from the shorts' own world.
entries.scriptStyle: The script is narration, not conversation, and every line must be performable as mime before it is written. Tom's line is the customer's doubt, spoken as the narrator reading Tom's face; Jerry's line is the answer, carrying one real, specific thing this business offers, spoken as the narrator reading Jerry's gesture. Keep the Telugu dry, warm and observational — the humour lives in the pause and the look, never in a pun — and let the closing line be the narrator inviting the viewer in over Jerry's open-handed welcome.
negatives: Do NOT restyle the environment into a cartoon — the location must stay photoreal

entries.label: Chhota Bheem & Chutki
entries.tagline: Homegrown and hearty — he asks it bluntly, she teases him and gives the real reason.
entries.franchise: the Indian animated television series "Chhota Bheem" (Green Gold Animation)

speakers.name: Chhota Bheem
speakers.voice: bright, hearty and open-chested, a boy's voice with real carry behind it
speakers.persona: brave, straightforward and generous, takes everything at face value and says exactly what he sees; no cunning in him at all
speakers.scriptRole: Opens every clip. He asks the customer's real question the blunt way a straightforward person asks it, and reacts with open admiration. He never delivers the offer or the call to action.

speakers.name: Chutki
speakers.voice: quick, clear and lightly teasing, a half-step brighter than his and noticeably faster
speakers.persona: sharp, practical and well-informed, gently teases him for not knowing, and is always the one who actually checked; warm underneath the teasing
speakers.scriptRole: Answers Bheem in every clip. She carries the business value — the service, the offer, the proof — usually with a small tease before the fact, and delivers the closing call to action in the final clip.

entries.styleDirective: 2D television-animation characters in the flat, bright Indian TV style the series is drawn in, composited into a PHOTOREAL live-action environment. The characters stay cartoon; the location stays photographic, is never restyled and is never turned into a village set. They stand on the actual floor at believable scale against real fixtures, casting soft contact shadows that match the scene's light.

entries.voiceDirection: Bheem's voice sits open and forward with air behind it — he never mutters; Chutki answers faster, brighter and slightly clipped so her tease lands before her fact does. Keep a clear gap between the two lines — a beat where he realises he was wrong — and let her final line in the ad slow right down and warm up, the tease dropped, only the invitation left. Clean studio recording, no reverb, no narrator, no crowd.
entries.expressionDirection: Bheem opens with lifted brows and a wide uncomplicated grin of admiration, mouth open on the question; when she corrects him his brows knit for exactly one beat and then the grin returns bigger than before. Chutki starts on a knowing sideways look and a small smirk, and blooms into an open smile as she gives the real reason. On the closing clip both faces are straight-on, proud and welcoming, with the smirk gone from hers.
entries.eyeDirection: Bheem's eyes go straight to the biggest, most impressive thing in the shot and stay there while he asks, then swing to Chutki on her first word. Chutki looks at him sideways for the tease, out to the real product or counter as she names the reason, then back to him. In the final clip she takes the lens first and holds it through the call to action while he turns in beside her a beat later.
entries.gestureDirection: Bheem gestures wide and two-handed — arms opening to take in the size of the place, one flat hand tapped against the other when he is impressed — always with the palm, never a jabbing finger. Chutki gestures small and fast: one finger up on the tease, a flat hand turned towards the real shelf or counter on the fact, then both hands clasped in front of her. Her closing gesture is a single unhurried open palm towards the viewer.
entries.bodyLanguage: Bheem stands wide and settled with his weight even and his chest open, and leans back slightly when impressed rather than forward — he takes the place in. Chutki stands lighter, angled towards him with one hip set, and steps a half pace forward on her fact so she owns the middle of the frame for that beat. In the closing frame they stand shoulder to shoulder, front-on, with the premises spread wide behind them.
entries.cameraDirection: Set the lens a touch below the pair's eye line so they read as capable and the premises rise behind them, matched to the client photograph's own perspective. Static medium two-shot with real depth — the shop's own aisle, doorway or counter line running back into frame — and both characters clearly separated. At most one slow push-in on the proof clip; hold everything else and let their footwork carry the change.

It stays a real working Indian shop with real wear — never a render, and never Dholakpur, a village set or anything from the show's own world.

Bheem's line is short, plain and admiring, always a question or an exclamation and never a fact; Chutki's line is a quick half-line tease followed by one specific real detail taken from the business information. The humour is the difference in how confidently the two of them know things, never wordplay and never at the client's expense. The final line is Chutki's, tease dropped, telling the viewer plainly to come.

entries.label: Mickey & Minnie
entries.tagline: Warm and courteous hosts — no bickering, just two well-loved characters welcoming the viewer in.
entries.franchise: the Walt Disney animated shorts and series featuring "Mickey Mouse" and "Minnie Mouse"

speakers.name: Mickey
speakers.voice: high, bright and buoyant, with a chuckle sitting just under every line
speakers.persona: cheerful, curious and unfailingly polite, delighted by small things, a natural showman who presents rather than argues
speakers.scriptRole: Opens every clip. He asks the customer's real question as a delighted discovery about something genuinely in the premises. He never delivers the offer or the call to action.

speakers.name: Minnie
speakers.voice: sweet, lilting and gracious, warm and a shade slower than his
speakers.persona: welcoming, poised and quietly in charge of the room, the host who makes a stranger feel expected; kind and encouraging, never gushing
speakers.scriptRole: Answers Mickey in every clip. She carries the business value — the service, the offer, the proof — the way a hostess explains her own home, and delivers the closing call to action in the final clip.

entries.styleDirective: Classic Disney 2D animation characters with their own clean rounded line and shading, composited into a PHOTOREAL live-action environment. The characters stay drawn; the location stays photographic and is never given a Disney makeover, a sparkle pass or a storybook grade. They stand on the actual floor in correct perspective, casting soft contact shadows that match the scene's light.
entries.dialogueRhythm: Mickey speaks first, delighted and curious, offering the customer's question as something he has just discovered; Minnie answers with the business value, courteous and unhurried, the way a host explains her own home. There is no bickering and no one is the fool — the comedy is shared delight, each of them enjoying the other's enthusiasm. This order never reverses, and both characters speak in every single clip.
entries.voiceDirection: Both voices stay high, light and musical but never on the same note: Mickey lands bright and forward with a laugh underneath, Minnie answers a shade lower, slower and rounder, so the pair read as a duet rather than an echo. Nothing is ever shouted and nothing is ever hard-sold — the whole ad sits at the volume of two hosts welcoming you into a room. The closing line is Minnie's, slowest of all, with the smile audible on the last word. Clean studio recording, no reverb, no narrator, no laugh track.
entries.expressionDirection: Mickey plays every clip with high brows and a wide open smile that grows on the discovery, plus one clean surprised take — mouth open, cheeks up — timed to the exact word that names the product. Minnie holds a gracious closed-mouth smile with her head tilted slightly, and opens into a warm full smile across the last third of her line. Neither face ever goes neutral; the change is between two grades of delight, and the final clip has both beaming straight at the viewer.
entries.eyeDirection: Mickey's eyes sweep the real premises — up to the high shelf, along the counter — before settling on Minnie for his question, and he flicks to the lens for a fraction of a second on his last word, sharing the moment with the viewer. Minnie's gaze stays on Mickey for the first half of her answer, moves once to the real thing she is naming, and comes to camera for the whole of the closing line. Their eyes meet at least once in every clip.
entries.gestureDirection: Mickey presents rather than points: an open upturned palm swept towards whatever he is asking about, both hands rising together on the surprise, hands returning to a light clasp between beats. Minnie's gestures are smaller and hostess-like — one hand turned gracefully towards the counter or display as she names it, the other resting easily — and on the closing line both her hands open outward to the viewer in a full welcome. No jabbing, no chopping, nothing frantic anywhere in the ad.
entries.bodyLanguage: Both stand upright and lightly bouncy on the balls of their feet, weight even, turned about a third towards each other and the rest towards the viewer — theatrical hosting, not casual chat. Mickey takes the half step forward when he asks; Minnie holds her ground and lets him come to her. Close the ad with the two of them side by side and square to camera, a small shared beat of stillness before the invitation.
entries.cameraDirection: Compose theatrically: the pair centred and balanced with the business's best real feature framed cleanly between or behind them, lens at eye level, horizon level — no dutch, no oddity. Movement is at most one gentle continuous dolly-in across the clip, otherwise locked, and the closing shot opens a little wider to give the welcome room. Keep the composition symmetric enough to feel designed without turning the shop into a stage set.
entries.backgroundDirection: With no client photographs, build the best-presented honest version of exactly this business — swept floor, stock fronted up, a tidy counter, bright even daylight with warm fill, everything reading clean and cared for while still being an actual Indian shop with real fixtures and real wear. Never a theme park, never a castle, never a Disney-styled interior: the only charm in the frame is the client's own.

No bickering, no put-downs, no jokes at anyone's expense — the warmth is the joke — and the closing line is Minnie's personal invitation, spoken as if to one person.
