entries.label: Lilo & Stitch
entries.tagline: Built for family-run businesses — an honest child, a chaotic best friend, and "we look after our own" as the whole pitch.
entries.franchise: the Disney animated feature and series "Lilo & Stitch"

speakers.name: Lilo
speakers.voice: earnest and slightly husky, a real child's voice, sincere and matter-of-fact with no sing-song in it
speakers.persona: odd, honest and big-hearted, says the true thing without softening it, treats every stranger as family already
speakers.scriptRole: Opens every clip. She asks the customer's real question with disarming, unembarrassed directness — the thing an adult would be too polite to ask. She never delivers the offer or the call to action.

speakers.name: Stitch
speakers.voice: gravelly, clipped and chirping, bursty and rough but landing every word clearly
speakers.persona: chaotic, delighted and physical, curious about everything, softening into fierce loyalty; understands far more than he lets on
speakers.scriptRole: Answers Lilo in every clip. He carries the business value — the service, the offer, the proof — in short rough bursts that add up, and delivers the closing call to action in the final clip, slow and clean enough for a stranger to catch first time.

entries.styleDirective: Hand-drawn Disney feature-animation characters, soft-edged and expressive exactly as the film draws them, composited into a PHOTOREAL live-action environment. The characters stay drawn; the location stays photographic and is never washed into watercolour or repainted in the film's own background style. Both make real contact with the floor and fixtures, casting soft shadows that match the room's light.
entries.dialogueRhythm: Lilo speaks first, asking with disarming honesty; Stitch answers in short broken growly bursts that add up to the business's value, and the run of rough energy always resolves on one clear, plainly spoken line. This order never reverses. His closing invitation must be clean enough for a stranger to understand the first time, however rough everything before it sounded. Both characters speak in every single clip.
entries.voiceDirection: Lilo is recorded close and dry — a real child, a little husky, completely sincere, never cute-voiced. Stitch is the opposite: gravelly, compressed and bursty, riding low with sudden upward chirps, and he must stay intelligible however rough he sounds — if a word of his closing line is lost, the take is wrong. Keep the two textures far apart, the smooth child against the growl, and let the final clip drop the chaos so the invitation lands warm and slow. Clean studio recording, no reverb, no narrator, no pitch-shifting or alien processing on Stitch.
entries.expressionDirection: Lilo asks with a flat, serious, unblinking face — no cuteness at all — and only breaks into a small crooked smile after Stitch has answered. Stitch runs the other way: ears and brows up in mischief, a wide toothy grin mid-line, then a sudden soft-eyed sincere look on his last two or three words, and that softening is the beat that actually sells the business. In the closing clip both hold still for once — Lilo smiling properly, Stitch open and warm at the lens.
entries.eyeDirection: Lilo looks straight at the real thing she is asking about, then straight at Stitch, with long steady blinks and no darting — her stillness is what makes her funny. Stitch's eyes go everywhere first, scanning the shelves and the ceiling, then snap to the lens and stay there for the final words of his line. On the last clip Stitch takes the camera first and Lilo joins him a beat later, both holding through the call to action.
entries.gestureDirection: Lilo gestures rarely and plainly: one flat hand pointed at what she means, then dropped to her side. Stitch is all hands — a fast double tap on the real counter or shelf he is naming, a two-handed grab that stops just short of picking anything up, arms thrown wide on his best word — and then everything goes still for his closing line, both hands opening slowly towards the viewer. He may touch and lean on the client's fixtures; he never lifts, throws or damages anything.
entries.bodyLanguage: Lilo stands square, still and grounded, hands often at her sides — she is the calm one in the frame. Stitch stays low and forward-leaning, crouched on the real floor or braced against a real fixture, weight shifting constantly, popping up onto two feet only when he answers. Keep him small and close to the ground so the height difference reads, and end the ad with Stitch settling in against Lilo's side, both facing the viewer — the family idea shown rather than stated.
entries.cameraDirection: Shoot closer and warmer than the other packs: a tight two-shot at Lilo's eye level with a soft tilt down to include Stitch, using the shop's own depth so it feels like standing in the room with them. A breath of hand-held stillness is welcome — movement you can feel but not see, never a shake — and any actual move is one slow settle towards the pair. Low warm light raking in from the front of the premises is the look, and it must stay a real room rather than a set.
entries.backgroundDirection: With no client photographs, build a family-run version of exactly this trade — the personal, lived-in kind of premises where the same family clearly works the counter, with real stock, real clutter in the corners and warm late-afternoon light raking low through the doorway. It stays an ordinary Indian business: no Hawaii, no beach, no palms, no tropical décor and nothing from the film's own island.
entries.scriptStyle: Sincere, plain spoken Telugu with no cleverness in it at all. Lilo's line is an honest, slightly blunt question a real child would ask and it never softens itself; Stitch answers in short bursts of simple words that add up to one real, specific thing this business does, with the last burst a full clean sentence anyone can follow. Family is the running idea — this is a place that looks after people — and the closing line is Stitch's short warm invitation, spoken slower than everything before it.

entries.label: SpongeBob & Patrick
entries.tagline: Loud, bright and scroll-stopping — a manic question, then a slow answer that turns out to be the smartest line in the ad.
entries.franchise: the American animated television series "SpongeBob SquarePants" (Nickelodeon)

speakers.name: SpongeBob
speakers.voice: high, nasal and bursting with enthusiasm, cracking upward on every excited word
speakers.persona: boundlessly optimistic and eager to please, treats everything in front of him as the best thing he has ever seen, and means it every time
speakers.scriptRole: Opens every clip. He asks the customer's real question at twice the necessary volume, thrilled by something genuinely in the premises. He never delivers the offer or the call to action.

speakers.name: Patrick
speakers.voice: slow, thick and dopey, dropping low and dragging the last word of the sentence
speakers.persona: slow, guileless, wrong about nearly everything and then accidentally exactly right; never in a hurry and never embarrassed
speakers.scriptRole: Answers SpongeBob in every clip. He arrives at the business value the long way round and lands it dead right, and delivers the closing call to action in the final clip — plain, slow and surprisingly clear.

entries.styleDirective: Thick-outlined 2D cartoon characters in the show's own flat, saturated drawing style, composited into a PHOTOREAL live-action environment. The characters stay cartoon; the location stays photographic and is never given an underwater cast, a bubble layer or an aquatic grade. They stand on the actual dry floor in correct perspective, casting soft contact shadows that match the scene's light.
entries.dialogueRhythm: SpongeBob speaks first, over-thrilled, firing off the customer's question far louder than it needed to be asked; Patrick answers slowly, and the joke is that the dim one says the sharpest thing in the ad. The beat is fixed — manic question, long unhurried answer — and the pause before Patrick starts is part of the comedy, never a mistake. This order never reverses, and both characters speak in every single clip.
entries.voiceDirection: SpongeBob is recorded hot, high and nasal, cracking upward on his last word, and he starts each clip a half-beat early because he cannot wait. Patrick answers from the bottom of the range, slow and thick, with a genuine pause dropped mid-line where he appears to lose the thread and then find it again. The gap between the two speeds IS the joke, so never let Patrick catch up or SpongeBob calm down — except on the final line, where Patrick stays slow but turns unexpectedly clear and direct. Clean studio recording, no reverb, no narrator, no bubble or underwater treatment on the voices.
entries.expressionDirection: SpongeBob plays one huge take per clip: eyes going wide and round, mouth stretching into a full open grin exactly on the word that names the product, brows shooting up. Patrick starts slack, half-lidded and entirely blank, and holds it for longer than is comfortable, then a slow single-brow lift and a small proud smile as his answer lands. Never let both faces be big at once — one is exploding while the other is empty, and that contrast is the entire performance.
entries.eyeDirection: SpongeBob's eyes lock onto the real product or display, widen, then swing to Patrick and back twice inside a single line, and he finds the lens on his last word every time. Patrick's eyes stay unfocused and pointed vaguely upward for the first half of his line, then drop, focus and land on his own pointing hand before he turns, unhurried, to the camera. On the closing clip both look straight down the lens — SpongeBob beaming, Patrick blinking once, slowly.
entries.gestureDirection: SpongeBob's arms work constantly: both hands flung wide, then clasped under his chin, then a fast two-handed present towards the real shelf or counter, all inside one line. Patrick moves once — a single slow heavy arm rising to point flat at the thing he means, held there while he finishes, then dropped. On the last clip SpongeBob's hands come together in delight and Patrick's one arm opens outward to the viewer: the slowest gesture in the ad, and the one carrying the invitation.
entries.bodyLanguage: SpongeBob bounces on the spot, up on his toes, leaning in and springing back on the take, but always landing on the real floor with the same contact shadow. Patrick stands flat-footed and fully settled, and does not move at all — he may sway once. Stage them with a clear gap between so the difference in energy reads instantly, and close with both squared to camera, SpongeBob bouncing to a stop just before Patrick speaks.
entries.cameraDirection: Play it broad and bright: a slightly wide medium two-shot with generous headroom so SpongeBob's takes have somewhere to go, lens at eye level, the client's most colourful real stock filling the space behind them. Keep the camera locked — this comedy is timing, not movement — and allow at most one quick small push-in on the take beat of a single clip. Frame Patrick with a touch more empty space than he needs; the emptiness around him is funny.
entries.backgroundDirection: With no client photographs, build the brightest honest version of exactly this business — dense, colourful, well-lit real stock, high-key frontal daylight, everything readable at a glance by a viewer scrolling fast. It must stay a real, dry, Indian shop floor: no underwater look, no bubbles, no water light, no aquatic props and nothing from Bikini Bottom.
entries.scriptStyle: Big, simple spoken Telugu — short exclamatory words, nothing subtle, everything at the front of the mouth. SpongeBob's line is an over-thrilled question about something genuinely in the shop; Patrick's line takes the long way round and then states one real, specific thing the business offers in the plainest words available. The gag is that the slow one says the smartest thing, so Patrick's answer must never be wrong or nonsense — it is exactly right, just late. The closing line is Patrick's: short, slow and unarguable.

entries.label: Oggy & Jack
entries.tagline: Fast slapstick energy without a single broken thing — a panic, a yelp, and a flat confident answer.
entries.franchise: the French animated television series "Oggy and the Cockroaches" (Xilam Animation)

speakers.name: Oggy
speakers.voice: light, elastic and put-upon, closer to a yelp than to speech, every line starting out of a sound
speakers.persona: easy-going and house-proud, wants a quiet life, panics instantly and recovers just as fast, embarrassed about neither
speakers.scriptRole: Opens every clip. He asks the customer's real question in its panicked form — the worry said out loud before it has been thought through. He never delivers the offer or the call to action.

speakers.name: Jack
speakers.voice: brisk, brassy and confident, faster and lower than his, arriving on the beat and closing the subject
speakers.persona: hot-tempered cousin, inventive and decisive, absolutely certain he knows best — and in this shop he genuinely does
speakers.scriptRole: Answers Oggy in every clip. He carries the business value — the service, the offer, the proof — delivered as if the matter is now settled, and delivers the closing call to action in the final clip.

entries.styleDirective: Glossy French 2D animation characters with their own smooth rubbery line exactly as the series draws them, composited into a PHOTOREAL live-action environment. The characters stay cartoon; the location stays photographic, is never restyled into a cartoon house and is never flattened to match them. They stand on the actual floor in correct perspective, casting soft contact shadows that match the scene's light.
entries.dialogueRhythm: Oggy and Jack never speak words in the original — they yelp, gasp and mutter — so their lines here are kept as close to that as speech allows: every line begins from a sound they would really make and stays short, loud and reactive. Oggy speaks first, flapping at the customer's question; Jack cuts straight in with the answer and takes charge of the room. This order never reverses, and both characters speak in every single clip.
entries.voiceDirection: Both voices are cartoon-thin and elastic, pitched above a normal speaking voice, and each line starts from a sound rather than a word — Oggy's small startled yelp, Jack's impatient grunt — with the sentence tumbling straight out of it. Oggy runs light, fluttery and rising, always slightly out of breath; Jack is lower, brassier and flatter, landing on the beat. Volume is high but never harsh, and the final line drops the panic completely: Jack, slower and friendlier than anywhere else in the ad. Clean studio recording, no reverb, no narrator, no cartoon sound effects on the voice track.
entries.expressionDirection: Oggy plays alarm and relief inside the same clip: eyes huge and round with brows up on the question, mouth pulled wide, then everything softening into a foolish relieved grin the instant Jack answers — and that switch is a snap, one beat worried and the next delighted, never a fade. Jack holds one confident, slightly smug half-smile with a single raised brow for his entire line, and only breaks it into a genuine open smile at the very end of the ad.
entries.eyeDirection: Oggy's eyes dart — to the real product, to the door, back to the product, then to Jack — an unsettled scan that stops dead the moment Jack starts talking. Jack barely moves his eyes: a steady look at Oggy, one deliberate glance at the real thing he is naming, then a straight look into the lens on the closing line. In the last clip Oggy finally stops darting and finds the camera too, half a beat behind Jack.
entries.gestureDirection: Oggy's hands flap near his face and chest, palms up in helpless question, one hand tapping the other on his loudest word — fast, wide and slightly useless. Jack gestures once, decisively: a flat hand laid towards the real counter, machine or shelf as he names it, and held there, never repeated inside the same clip. Nothing is picked up, thrown or knocked over — the hands stay in the air or on the character.
entries.bodyLanguage: Oggy is springy and vertical — up on his toes, recoiling from a surprise, hands raised — but always resettling on the real floor with a matching contact shadow. Jack plants himself with his weight forward and shoulders squared, moving only to take one step towards the thing he is talking about. Stage them tight, almost shoulder to shoulder, the way two relatives argue in a doorway, and end with both turned out to the viewer and Oggy calm at last.
entries.cameraDirection: Stage it flat and frontal in the French cartoon manner: a locked, level, slightly wide two-shot with both characters full-figure against a clean horizontal line in the premises — a counter edge, a shelf run, a doorway. No dutch, no drift, no hand-held; the frame holds and the pair play the whole scene inside it. If a move is used at all, make it one crisp short push-in on the clip that names the offer, then return to a wider calmer frame for the close.
entries.backgroundDirection: With no client photographs, build an unusually spotless version of exactly this business — polished floor, everything squared up and put away, clean hard light throwing crisp shadows — because this comedy needs a room that looks like somebody has just finished cleaning it. It stays authentic Indian premises for this trade with real stock and real fixtures: never a domestic house interior and nothing from the show's own world.
entries.scriptStyle: Short, loud, reactive spoken Telugu — exclamations more than sentences, nothing longer than a person would shout across a room. Oggy's line is the panicked version of the customer's question; Jack's line is the flat confident answer carrying one real, specific detail from the business information, said as if the matter is now closed. The humour is pure reaction and timing, never wordplay and never at the client's expense. The final line is Jack's, calm and welcoming — the only unhurried thing either of them says.

entries.label: Ben 10 & Grandpa Max
entries.tagline: Kid dares, grandfather settles it — the pick for workshops, service centres and anything that has to feel proven.
entries.franchise: the Cartoon Network animated series "Ben 10", in its original series look

speakers.name: Ben 10
speakers.voice: cocky, energetic and fast, a ten-year-old's voice cracking upward on the boastful word
speakers.persona: confident to the point of cheeky, restless, convinced he already knows, and genuinely good underneath the attitude
speakers.scriptRole: Opens every clip. He throws out the customer's real question as a challenge — "is that even worth it?" — and never states a fact. He never delivers the offer or the call to action.

speakers.name: Grandpa Max
speakers.voice: gravelly, calm and grandfatherly, slow and completely certain
speakers.persona: seasoned and unflappable, has been everywhere and tried everything and says so without boasting; dry humour, no lectures
speakers.scriptRole: Answers Ben in every clip. He carries the business value — the service, the offer, the proof — framed as something he has seen enough of life to judge, and delivers the closing call to action in the final clip.

entries.styleDirective: Angular action-cartoon 2D characters drawn exactly as the original series draws them, composited into a PHOTOREAL live-action environment. The characters stay cartoon; the location stays photographic and is never given sci-fi lighting, glow or a stylised grade. They stand on the actual floor in correct perspective, casting hard-edged contact shadows that match the scene's directional light.
entries.dialogueRhythm: Ben speaks first, cocky and impatient, throwing the customer's question out as a challenge; Grandpa Max answers slowly with the earned reason, and the beat is always "kid dares — grandfather settles it". A clear silence sits between the two lines and that silence is where the authority lives. This order never reverses, and both characters speak in every single clip.
entries.voiceDirection: Ben is recorded bright, fast and forward — a ten-year-old talking over the end of the previous line, cracking upward when he boasts. Grandpa Max answers a full register lower, gravelly and slow, with a small dry chuckle before the fact lands; he never raises his voice and never sounds like an advertisement. Keep a clear beat of silence between Ben's challenge and Max's answer, and let Max's closing line be the slowest and warmest thing in the ad. Clean studio recording, no reverb, no narrator, no processing or sci-fi treatment on either voice.
entries.expressionDirection: Ben opens with a cocky half-smile and one raised brow, chin up, and lets it collapse into genuine wide-eyed surprise the moment Max produces the fact — the collapse is the gag and it must land on a specific word, never drift in gradually. Max holds a calm amused crinkled-eye look throughout, a knowing half-smile that never becomes a grin, and softens into open warmth on the final line. In the closing clip Ben drops the attitude completely and gives the lens an honest grin beside his grandfather.
entries.eyeDirection: Ben's eyes flick fast — a dismissive glance at the real product, a sideways look at Max, then back with a double-take when he is proved wrong — and he hits the lens on his last word as if checking whether the viewer saw that. Max's gaze is slow and settled: on the real equipment or stock he is talking about, then across to Ben, then straight into the lens for the whole call to action, held without a blink. Their eye-lines cross clearly once in every clip.
entries.gestureDirection: Ben gestures fast and loose — a hand thrown out towards whatever he is questioning, arms folded for a beat while he waits, then both palms up in defeat. Max uses one hand, slowly: resting it on the counter or the real machine he is naming, or turning it palm-up towards it, and it never hurries. On the closing line Max's open hand comes towards the viewer while Ben's hands stay down — one clear invitation, not two competing ones. Neither character ever touches, raises or points at his own wrist.
entries.bodyLanguage: Ben is restless: weight shifting, one shoulder dropped, half turning away and coming back, but always in full contact with the real floor. Max stands still and heavy with his feet planted, and leans in only once per clip, towards the thing he is proving. Play the difference between them through staging and depth without describing either of them, and finish with Ben stepping in beside Max, both squared to camera for the invitation.
entries.cameraDirection: Give it adventure-series energy without breaking the frame: a medium two-shot from slightly below eye level with real depth behind — an aisle, a service bay, a lit doorway — and hard directional light making genuine shadows on the real floor. The camera holds and the movement lives in the staging; allow one slow steady push-in on the clip that carries the proof, then finish wider and level with the business unmistakable around them.
entries.backgroundDirection: With no client photographs, build the working, hands-on version of exactly this business — the service side, the workbench, the stocked back wall, the roller shutter half up with hard daylight cutting across a floor that has actually been worked on. Real tools, real wear, real Indian premises for this exact trade: never a garage from the show, never the Rust Bucket, and no sci-fi, laboratory or spaceship dressing anywhere in frame.
entries.scriptStyle: Everyday spoken Telugu with a generation gap audible in it. Ben's line is short, cocky and challenging — the customer's doubt thrown out as a dare — and it never states a fact; Max's line answers with one real, specific thing this business does, framed as something he has seen enough of life to judge, so it sounds earned rather than advertised. The humour is the kid being outclassed by his grandfather, never sarcasm at the client's expense. The closing line is Max's, unhurried and addressed personally to the viewer.
